title: Strange life cycles: seventeen years underground, one journey home, and a jellyfish that starts again

summary.text: One kind of cicada lives underground for seventeen years, then sings for about four weeks. Why would any animal live like this? In this unit you will test whether it is safer to come out alone or in a crowd, and how weak a smell your nose can follow home.
summary.art: Three small scenes side by side: a cicada climbing out of a hole under a tree at dusk, a red salmon leaping up a waterfall, and a tiny bell-shaped jellyfish with a curved arrow pointing back to a small polyp on a rock.

intro.hook: Think of a cicada, a mayfly, a hen, an elephant and yourself. Which one spends the biggest share of life as a youngster? Say what you think, and why.
intro.text: Most people pick the elephant or the human, because our childhoods feel long. In the first activity, Life Bars, you draw each life as a bar and measure the answer. Then you meet three animals whose life cycles seem strange to us. For each one you ask the same question. What dangers and what food would make this way of living work?
intro.art: A child at a table drawing five long bars on paper with a ruler, with small drawings of a cicada, a mayfly, a hen, an elephant and a girl beside the bars.

outcomes: By the end I can describe the life cycles of a periodical cicada, a Pacific salmon and the immortal jellyfish, and say what is unusual in each.
By the end I can explain how coming out in a crowd protects each animal, using my own test results.
By the end I can explain how a salmon finds her home stream, and give the evidence.
By the end I can say why some animals breed once and die, and others breed many times.
By the end I can explain why some animals have millions of young and others have one, using the egg budget and survival curves.
By the end I can say what the immortal jellyfish's cells do, and why 'immortal' is not quite the right word.
By the end I can run a fair test with a model, and say what the model leaves out.
By the end I can say what scientists still argue about or do not know about these life cycles.

terms.meaning: The timetable of a life says how long each stage lasts, and when and how often the animal breeds.
terms.example: A hen starts laying at about five months old. A periodical cicada breeds only once, at seventeen years.
terms.art: Two bars of the same length, one marked 'hen' with a short first part, one marked 'cicada' with a very long first part.

terms.meaning: A nymph is the young of an insect that has no pupa stage. A nymph grows by shedding their skin several times.
terms.example: A cicada nymph lives underground and drinks sap from tree roots.
terms.art: A brown, wingless cicada nymph with strong digging front legs, in a small burrow beside a root.

terms.meaning: A periodical cicada is a cicada whose whole population grows up together and comes out in the same year, after a fixed number of years.
terms.example: The periodical cicadas of the eastern United States come out after 13 or 17 years. One kind in Meghalaya comes out every 4 years.
terms.art: A black cicada with red eyes and orange wing veins sitting on a leaf.

terms.meaning: A brood is all the periodical cicadas of one region that come out in the same year.
terms.example: In 2024 a 13-year brood and a 17-year brood came out in the same year in the United States.
terms.art: A map with two shaded patches and a year written on each patch.

terms.meaning: To emerge is to come out. For a cicada it means digging up out of the soil to become an adult.
terms.example: Millions of cicadas emerge within a few evenings.
terms.art: Many small round holes in the soil under a tree, with nymphs climbing the trunk.

terms.meaning: Predator satiation means that so many prey arrive together that the predators eat until they are full, and most prey are left alive.
terms.example: Winged termites fly out together after the first rain. Crows, geckos and frogs eat many, and most still escape.
terms.art: A fat bird on a branch looking away from a tree trunk covered in cicadas.

terms.meaning: A prime number is a whole number bigger than 1 that can be divided exactly only by 1 and by itself.
terms.example: 13 and 17 are prime numbers. 12 is not, because 2, 3, 4 and 6 divide it exactly.
terms.art: The numbers 12 to 18 in a row, with 13 and 17 circled.

terms.meaning: To spawn is to release eggs or sperm into the water. A sperm is the tiny cell from the male that joins with an egg to start a new life.
terms.example: A female salmon spawns in a nest she digs in the gravel of a stream.
terms.art: A female salmon lying on her side over a hollow in river gravel, with orange eggs in the hollow.

terms.meaning: A smolt is a young salmon whose body has changed so that they can live in salt water.
terms.example: A smolt turns silver and swims down the river to the sea.
terms.art: A small silver salmon swimming downstream past river plants.

terms.meaning: Imprinting is fast learning at one stage of life that lasts for the rest of that life.
terms.example: A young salmon imprints on the smell of their home stream before they leave for the sea.
terms.art: A young salmon in a stream with wavy smell lines drifting from the rocks and plants to the fish's nose.

terms.meaning: Osmosis is the movement of water through a thin skin, from the side with less salt towards the side with more salt.
terms.example: A potato strip in very salty water goes soft, because water leaves the potato's cells.
terms.art: Two tumblers, one with a stiff potato strip in plain water and one with a bent potato strip in salty water.

terms.meaning: A semelparous animal breeds only once in their life and then dies.
terms.example: Pacific salmon, mayflies and octopuses are semelparous.
terms.art: A single tall bar on a time line, labelled 'breeds once'.

terms.meaning: An iteroparous animal breeds many times in their life.
terms.example: Hens, elephants, crows and humans are iteroparous.
terms.art: Several short bars spread along a time line, labelled 'breeds many times'.

terms.meaning: A survival curve is a line graph that shows how many animals out of a starting group are still alive at each age.
terms.example: The survival curve of a fish drops almost to zero in the first weeks. An elephant's curve stays high for many years.
terms.art: A graph with three lines: one that stays high and then falls, one that falls steadily, and one that drops at once.

terms.meaning: A medusa is the swimming, bell-shaped stage of a jellyfish. It is the adult stage, which makes eggs or sperm.
terms.example: The jellyfish you see washed up on a beach are medusae.
terms.art: A bell-shaped jellyfish with tentacles hanging down, swimming.

terms.meaning: A polyp is the stage of a jellyfish that stays fixed to a rock or a shell. A polyp looks like a tiny stalk with a ring of tentacles on top.
terms.example: A jellyfish polyp grows buds, and each bud swims away as a small medusa.
terms.art: A tiny stalk fixed to a rock with a ring of tentacles on top and small buds on its side.

terms.meaning: A cell is the smallest living part of a body. Your body is made of about thirty trillion cells of about two hundred kinds.
terms.example: Skin cells, muscle cells and nerve cells are three kinds of cell.
terms.art: Three differently shaped cells side by side: a flat skin cell, a long muscle cell and a branching nerve cell.

terms.meaning: A gene is one instruction in a cell, written in a long molecule called DNA. A cell uses some of its genes and leaves the others switched off.
terms.example: A muscle cell and a skin cell carry the same genes, but they use different ones.
terms.art: A row of small switches inside a cell, some up and some down.

terms.meaning: Transdifferentiation is one kind of cell changing into another kind of cell.
terms.example: In the immortal jellyfish, cells of the bell can change into the cells of a polyp.
terms.art: A muscle cell with an arrow to a round plain cell and then an arrow to a stinging cell.

terms.meaning: Senescence is the slow wearing down of a body with age, which makes death more likely each year.
terms.example: An old dog who moves stiffly and falls ill more often is showing senescence.
terms.art: An old dog with a grey muzzle lying on a mat.

explanations.concept: Every life cycle has a timetable
explanations.definition: A life cycle is the set of stages an animal goes through until they have young of their own. Its timetable says how long each stage lasts, and when and how often the animal breeds.
explanations.description: In Class 3 and Class 4 you met the stages: egg, young and adult. Now look at the times. A human is a child for about a fifth of a life. A periodical cicada is a youngster for seventeen years and an adult for about four weeks. A mayfly may be an adult for one day. A Pacific salmon breeds once and dies. An elephant mother has a calf every four or five years, for about forty years. One small jellyfish can go from adult back to young. None of these timetables is the normal one. Each was shaped over millions of years by natural selection. Natural selection means that the animals whose way of living left the most surviving young passed that way of living on. So for every timetable that looks strange to us, we can ask a useful question. What dangers and what food made this timetable work?
examples: A hen can lay her first egg at about five months old and may live six years or more. Most of her life is adult life.
A mayfly nymph lives in a stream for about a year. The winged adult has no working mouth and lives for a day or two.
In Life Bars, the adult part of the cicada's bar was only about one millimetre long.
explanations.art: Five bars of equal length for five animals, each split into a 'young' part and an 'adult' part of very different sizes.

explanations.concept: The periodical cicada: seventeen years underground
explanations.definition: A periodical cicada is a cicada whose whole population grows up underground together and comes out in the same year, after a fixed number of years.
explanations.description: Cicadas are insects that suck plant sap. The males sing loudly. In most kinds of cicada, including the ones you hear in India in summer, some adults come out every year. Seven kinds in the eastern United States are different. A female cuts slits in a twig and lays her eggs there. After six to ten weeks the eggs hatch. The young are called nymphs, and each is smaller than a grain of rice. They drop to the ground and dig down. Each nymph pushes a sucking tube into a tree root and drinks xylem sap. Xylem sap is the watery liquid that rises from a tree's roots to the leaves. This sap holds very little food, which is one reason the nymphs grow so slowly. After 17 years, or 13 years for some kinds, the nymphs dig upward. They wait until the soil about 20 centimetres down warms to about 18 degrees Celsius. Then millions come up within a few evenings. Each climbs a tree trunk, splits the old skin down the back and pulls out as a winged adult. The adults sing, mate, lay eggs and die within about a month. All the cicadas of one region that come up in the same year are called a brood.
examples: India has one known periodical cicada, in the Ri-Bhoi district of Meghalaya. They come out every four years. Sudhanya Ray Hajong and Salmah Yaakop described them for science in 2013, and local people had known the timetable long before.
In 2024, a 13-year brood and a 17-year brood came out in the same spring in the United States. That had last happened in 1803.
In a big emergence there can be more than 300 cicadas for every square metre of ground under the trees.
explanations.art: A cutaway of soil under a tree: nymphs of different sizes drinking from roots at different depths, and one nymph digging up towards the surface.

explanations.concept: How does a cicada count the years?
explanations.definition: A cicada nymph counts years by the yearly changes in the sap of the tree they drink from.
explanations.description: Under the ground there is no summer sky and no winter to see. So how does a nymph know that seventeen years have passed? A tree's sap changes through the year. In spring, when the tree grows new leaves, the sap carries more food. In 2000, Richard Karban, Carrie Black and Steven Weinbaum tested whether the nymphs count these changes. They moved nymphs of a 17-year brood onto the roots of peach trees. The nymphs were 15 years old. Then the scientists made the peach trees grow leaves and flowers twice in one year. The cicadas came out one year early. They had counted two springs in one calendar year. So a nymph counts the tree's yearly cycles and not the days. Nobody yet knows where in the body the count is kept, or how it is kept right up to seventeen.
examples: A cicada nymph on a tree that flowers twice in a year counts two years.
All the nymphs of a brood count the same trees' seasons. This is how millions of separate animals reach seventeen in the same spring.
The last signal is warmth. The nymphs wait just below the surface until the soil reaches about 18 degrees Celsius.
explanations.art: A nymph on a root with a small tally of marks beside them, and above the ground a tree shown four times: in leaf, bare, in leaf, bare.

explanations.concept: Safety in a crowd: predator satiation
explanations.definition: Predator satiation means that so many prey arrive together that the predators eat until they are full, and most of the prey are left alive.
explanations.description: A periodical cicada has no sting, no poison and no speed. Birds, squirrels, snakes, dogs and even fish eat them. Yet most survive, because a bird can eat only so many in a day. In one large emergence that scientists measured, birds ate about 15 of every 100 cicadas. Cicadas that come out in small numbers, or in the wrong year, are almost all eaten. You saw the same thing in the Crowd Test. The picker took about the same number of rajma in ten seconds, whether ten were on the towel or eighty. So the share eaten fell as the crowd grew. The long wait helps too. Predators cannot build up their numbers on a food that comes once in seventeen years. If the cicadas came out every year, more of the birds' chicks would be fed and would live. Then there would be more birds each year to eat cicadas.
examples: Winged termites pour out of the ground on the same evening after the first monsoon rain. Crows, geckos, frogs and people eat many, and most still fly on.
Olive ridley turtles nest in thousands on the same few nights at Rushikulya and Gahirmatha in Odisha. Jackals and dogs cannot dig up all the nests.
Many bamboos flower and seed together once in many years. Rats and birds cannot eat all the seed.
explanations.art: A tree trunk covered with hundreds of cicadas, and three birds on a branch with full bellies, not looking at them.

explanations.description: 13 and 17 are prime numbers. A prime number can be divided exactly only by 1 and by itself. No periodical cicada has a cycle of 12, 14, 15, 16 or 18 years. Scientists have three main ideas about why, and no agreed answer. In the game Emerge! you play with the first idea. Remember that it is only one idea.
examples: A 12-year cicada would meet a 2-year, a 3-year, a 4-year and a 6-year predator at every emergence. A 13-year cicada would meet each of them far less often.
A 13-year brood and a 17-year brood living in the same woods come out together only once in 221 years, because 13 times 17 is 221.
Some 17-year cicadas come out four years early, after 13 years. So the two cycles can change into each other.

perspectives.who: Hiding from predators that have cycles
perspectives.explanation: Suppose a predator or a parasite had good years every 2, 3 or 4 years. A cicada with a 12-year cycle would meet it every time. A cicada with a 13-year or 17-year cycle would meet it rarely. The scientist Stephen Jay Gould made this idea famous in 1977. The trouble is that nobody has found such a predator.

If cicadas with different cycles come out in the same year, they may mate with each other. Their young may then have mixed-up timetables and come out in small numbers, and be eaten. Prime cycles overlap very rarely. Jin Yoshimura and others have built this idea into mathematical models since 1997.

The cycles seem to change in jumps of four years. Cold periods in the past may have slowed growth and stretched the cycles step by step. On this view, 13 and 17 need no special reason. They may simply be where the jumps happened to stop.

explanations.art: A number line from 12 to 18 with 13 and 17 circled, and small predator faces under the numbers that 2 or 3 divide exactly.

explanations.concept: The salmon: river, sea and home again
explanations.definition: A Pacific salmon hatches in a river, grows up in the sea, and swims back to the same river to spawn once and die. To spawn is to release eggs or sperm into the water.
explanations.description: A sockeye salmon begins as an orange egg the size of a pea, buried in the gravel of a cold stream. The egg hatches in late winter. The tiny fish, called an alevin, stays in the gravel and lives on a bag of yolk under their belly. When the yolk is used up, the young fish swims out to feed. After a year or two in a lake, the young salmon turns silver. Now they are called a smolt, and they swim down to the sea. In the North Pacific Ocean the salmon feeds and grows for two or three years, and swims thousands of kilometres. Then she turns back. She finds the mouth of her own river and stops eating. Her body turns red. She swims upstream against the current and leaps up waterfalls. Some sockeye in Idaho swim about 1,400 kilometres and climb about 2,000 metres. At the stream where she hatched, she digs a nest in the gravel with her tail. She lays about 3,000 eggs, and a male covers them with sperm. Within days or weeks both are dead.
examples: India has no wild salmon. The hilsa makes a similar journey. Hilsa live in the Bay of Bengal and swim up the Godavari, the Hooghly and the Padma in the monsoon to spawn. In Andhra Pradesh the river-run hilsa is called pulasa.
Unlike Pacific salmon, many hilsa and some Atlantic salmon swim back to the sea and spawn again in a later year.
Eels do the opposite. An Indian mottled eel grows up in rivers and ponds, then swims to the sea to spawn once and die.
explanations.art: A loop drawn on a map: a stream with eggs in gravel, a lake with small fish, a river to the sea, a big silver fish in the ocean, and a red fish swimming back up the same river.

explanations.definition: A salmon finds her home stream mainly by smell. As a young fish she learns the smell of her stream, and as an adult she follows it back.
explanations.description: Every stream has its own smell, from its rocks, soil and plants. A young salmon learns this smell at about the time they become a smolt. This fast, lasting learning is called imprinting. In 1954, Warren Wisby and Arthur Hasler tested the idea at a creek in the state of Washington, where the creek splits into two branches. They caught salmon that had already chosen a branch. They plugged the noses of half the fish with cotton. Then they let all the fish go again below the fork. The fish with open noses mostly chose their own branch again. The fish with plugged noses chose the branches almost at random. In the 1970s Hasler's team went further. They raised young salmon in water with a tiny amount of one chemical in it. Later they put that chemical into one stream, and the grown salmon swam into that stream. In the open ocean there is no stream smell to follow. There the salmon may use the Earth's magnetism, as a compass does. This is an idea with some evidence, and it is not settled.
examples: In the Home Stream Test you found the weakest smell that your nose could still pick out. A salmon's nose works on smells many thousands of times weaker.
A few salmon in every hundred swim into the wrong stream. These strays are how salmon reach new rivers.
Olive ridley turtles also return to the coast where they hatched. They seem to use the Earth's magnetism.
explanations.art: A river that forks into two branches, with fish with open noses turning into one branch and fish with small cotton plugs in their noses spreading into both.

explanations.concept: From fresh water to salt water: the body's salt switch
explanations.definition: Water moves through the thin skin of living cells towards the saltier side. This movement is called osmosis. A salmon's body must handle it one way in a river and the opposite way in the sea.
explanations.description: Salt is the main thing here, though sugar and other dissolved substances draw water in the same way. A fish's blood is about one third as salty as sea water. River water has almost no salt. In a river, water keeps moving into the fish through the thin skin of the gills. So a river fish hardly drinks, and passes a lot of watery urine. In the sea, water keeps moving out of the fish into the saltier sea. So a sea fish drinks sea water, and special cells in the gills pump the extra salt out. A salmon lives both ways. Before a young salmon reaches the sea, their gill cells change, so that they pump salt out and no longer take salt in. This change is what makes a smolt. When the adult returns to the river, the gills change back. Most fish can live only one way. A river fish such as a rohu, put into the sea, would lose too much water and die.
examples: In the Salt Switch, a potato strip in very salty water went soft, because water left the potato's cells.
Your fingers wrinkle in a long bath for a different reason. Nerves tighten the blood vessels under the skin.
Hilsa, salmon and eels can make the switch. Most of the fish in a pond or in the open sea cannot.
explanations.art: The same fish drawn twice: in a river with arrows of water going in and drops of urine going out, and in the sea with a small arrow of water going out and salt being pushed out at the gills.

explanations.concept: Breed once, or breed many times
explanations.definition: A semelparous animal breeds once and then dies. An iteroparous animal breeds many times.
explanations.description: A body has a limited supply of energy from food. The body spends it on growing, on repairing itself and on making young. A Pacific salmon spends everything on one spawning. She stops eating and turns her fat, and even some of her muscle, into eggs and into swimming. Why not keep some back and breed again? Think about her chances. To breed twice she would have to swim back down the river, survive two more years at sea and climb the river again. Very few would manage it. So the salmon that put everything into one spawning left more young than the salmon that held back. Over many generations, spending everything became the usual way. Where the journey is shorter or safer, breeding again pays. An elephant has a good chance of living through each year, so her body spends on repair and breeds many times. This is the best explanation scientists have. It fits most animals, though not every case.
examples: A female giant Pacific octopus guards her eggs for about six months without eating. She dies around the time they hatch.
Adult mayflies have no working mouths. They mate, lay eggs and die, often on the same day.
Crows, hens, cats, hilsa and humans are iteroparous.
explanations.art: Two time lines: one with a single very tall bar at the end labelled 'salmon', one with many small bars spread out labelled 'elephant'.

explanations.concept: A dead salmon feeds a forest
explanations.definition: The bodies of salmon that die after spawning carry food from the sea into rivers and forests.
explanations.description: A salmon builds nearly all of her body in the ocean. When she dies in a mountain stream, that body stays there. Bears and eagles carry salmon into the forest and leave parts uneaten. Insects, fungi and bacteria break the bodies down. Scientists can trace where the material goes. Nitrogen is a substance that all living things need to build their bodies. Nitrogen atoms come in a lighter kind and a slightly heavier kind. Sea food holds more of the heavier kind than land food does. Trees beside salmon streams hold extra heavy nitrogen, so part of each tree was once salmon. The young salmon gain too. The tiny water animals they eat grow well in a stream fed by their parents' bodies.
examples: In salmon rivers in Alaska and Canada, more than fifty kinds of animals feed on salmon or salmon eggs.
When a dam stops salmon from reaching a stream, the stream gets less food, and so do the trees beside it.
Olive ridley eggs that fail to hatch feed crabs, ants and the plants of the dune.
explanations.art: A bear dropping a half-eaten salmon under tall trees beside a stream, with small arrows from the fish into the soil and up into the tree roots.

explanations.concept: Why so many young? The egg budget
explanations.definition: A mother has a limited amount of material and energy to put into eggs. She can make a few big eggs or many small ones, and never many big ones.
explanations.description: In Class 4 you learned the key number. Where a population stays steady, about two young from each pair grow up to breed. That holds for elephants and for fish. So why does one animal lay millions of eggs? You saw the reason in the Egg Budget. One ball of dough made four big eggs or about fifty small ones. A big egg holds more food, so a big, strong baby hatches from it. A small egg gives a tiny baby with almost no food store. Where a mother can guard or feed her young, a few big ones do well. In the open sea a fish cannot guard eggs that drift away. There, tiny eggs in huge numbers work better, because a few will land by luck where there is food and no hungry mouth. One ocean sunfish was found to carry about 300 million eggs. A survival curve shows the result. For a fish the curve drops almost to zero in the first weeks. For an elephant it stays high for many years.
examples: A kiwi lays one egg at a time. The egg weighs about a fifth as much as the mother.
A tsetse fly is an insect that has one baby at a time. The young grows inside the mother and is fed on a liquid like milk.
A hilsa may lay more than a million eggs in a season and gives them no care.
explanations.art: A ball of dough beside two plates: one with four large dough eggs and one with about fifty tiny ones.

explanations.definition: If all the young of any animal lived and bred, their numbers would multiply again and again until there was no room or food left. So in every generation most young must die before they breed.
explanations.description: Take a pair of frogs who lay 1,000 eggs. If every egg grew up, there would be 500 pairs. If each of those pairs laid 1,000 eggs, the next generation would have 500,000 frogs, and the one after that 250 million. Growth by multiplying again and again is called exponential growth. Charles Darwin worked this out in 1859 for the slowest breeder he knew, the elephant. He found that one pair would have about 19 million living descendants after about 750 years. But the world is not full of elephants or frogs. So most young of every kind die before they breed. Which ones live is partly luck. It is also partly small differences between them, such as a slightly faster tadpole. Those differences are passed on to the next generation. Darwin's name for this was natural selection.
examples: A housefly can lay about 500 eggs, and the young can breed within two or three weeks in warm weather. Hunger, cold, spiders and birds keep the numbers down.
When wild rabbits were set free in Australia in 1859 and found few predators, their numbers grew to hundreds of millions within about sixty years.
Bacteria in warm milk can double every half hour or so. That is how a spoon of curd sets a whole pot overnight.
explanations.art: A drawing of two frogs, then a pond full of frogs, then a whole map covered in frogs, with a large question mark.

explanations.concept: The immortal jellyfish: a life cycle that can run backwards
explanations.definition: The medusa of one small jellyfish, Turritopsis dohrnii, can change back into a polyp, which is the young stage. Then the polyp grows new medusae.
explanations.description: First, the usual jellyfish life cycle. An egg and a sperm join in the sea. The egg grows into a tiny swimming larva. The larva settles on a rock or a shell and becomes a polyp, a small stalk with tentacles. The polyp grows buds, and each bud swims away as a small medusa. The medusa grows up, makes eggs or sperm and dies. Turritopsis dohrnii has one more path. Their medusa is about 4 millimetres wide. When this medusa is starved, hurt or old, their bell can shrink into a small ball. The ball sinks, sticks to the bottom and grows into a new polyp within about three days. The polyp then buds off new medusae. These medusae have exactly the same genes as the old one. In the laboratory this can happen again and again. 'Immortal' is still not the right word. In the sea these jellyfish are eaten by fish, sea slugs and other jellyfish, and they die of disease. Nobody has yet followed one animal through the change in the wild.
examples: The scientist Shin Kubota in Japan kept one colony that went from medusa back to polyp ten times in two years.
A few other jellyfish, including the moon jellyfish, have since been seen to do something similar in the laboratory.
The Life Bars drawing has no bar for this jellyfish, because their life has no fixed end to measure to.
explanations.art: A circle of stages: egg, swimming larva, polyp on a rock, small medusa, adult medusa, with one extra arrow curving back from the adult medusa to the polyp.

explanations.definition: Nearly every cell in a body carries the same full set of genes. What kind of cell it is depends on which genes are switched on.
explanations.description: A medusa has muscle cells, nerve cells and stinging cells. A polyp needs a different mix. When the medusa turns into a polyp, cells do not simply die and get replaced. Many of them change kind. A cell switches some genes off and others on, and becomes a different kind of cell. This is called transdifferentiation. For a long time scientists thought it could not happen. They thought that a cell which had become one kind had lost the instructions for being any other kind. In 1962, John Gurdon showed that this was wrong. He took the centre, called the nucleus, out of a gut cell of a tadpole. The nucleus is where the genes are kept. He put it into a frog egg whose own nucleus had been destroyed. Some of these eggs grew into whole tadpoles, and later into frogs. So the gut cell still held every instruction. In 2006, Shinya Yamanaka and Kazutoshi Takahashi found that switching on just four genes turns a mouse skin cell back into a cell that can become any kind. The jellyfish does this kind of thing with no help.
examples: Your skin cells and your nerve cells carry the same genes. They differ in which genes are switched on.
In Run It Backwards, you made a dough medusa into a ball and then into a polyp, with no dough added or taken away.
A newt can grow back a lost leg. Cells near the wound go back to a simpler state and then build the new leg.
explanations.art: A muscle cell and a nerve cell, each with the same row of switches inside, but with different switches turned on.

explanations.concept: Why do most bodies wear out?
explanations.description: Most animals show senescence. That means the body slowly wears down with age, so that death becomes more likely each year. The immortal jellyfish shows that this is not a law for every animal. So why do most bodies wear out? Scientists give different answers.
examples: A Pacific salmon's body breaks down within days of spawning. A landlocked sockeye who never goes to sea dies after spawning too.
A hydra, a tiny freshwater relative of jellyfish, showed no sign of ageing in a four-year laboratory study.
Humans, elephants and some whales live for many years after their last young is born.

perspectives.explanation: Repairing a body perfectly costs energy. In the wild most animals are killed by hunger, disease or predators long before perfect repair would matter. So bodies spend on breeding and repair themselves only well enough. Thomas Kirkwood set out this idea in 1977.
A gene that helps an animal when young and harms them when old will still spread, because many animals never reach old age. Over time such genes pile up. George Williams set out this idea in 1957.

Animals built like hydra and some jellyfish keep cells that can renew every part of the body. For them, wearing out may not be built in. Other scientists reply that we have not watched these animals for long enough to be sure.

explanations.art: Three animals on a line marked 'wears out fast' at one end and 'hardly wears out' at the other: a salmon, an elephant and a tiny hydra.

explanations.definition: Animals differ in every part of the timetable: when they grow up, whether they need a mate, and even which sex they are.
explanations.description: An axolotl is a salamander from lakes near Mexico City. Most salamanders lose their gills and walk onto land, as frogs do. An axolotl keeps their feathery gills, stays in the water and breeds while still in a young-looking body. An aphid is a small insect that sucks plant sap. In warm months a female aphid gives birth to live daughters with no father. Each daughter is a copy of her mother, and can be carrying her own daughters before she is born. A clownfish begins adult life as a male. When the one female of the group dies, the largest male changes into a female. Some killifish live in pools that dry up each year. The adults die, and the eggs wait in the dry mud for months until rain returns.
examples: Look under the young leaves of a hibiscus or an avarakkai plant. A cluster of aphids is usually one mother's family.
Clownfish live among the sea anemones of the coral reefs of Lakshadweep and the Andaman Islands.
The purple frog of the Western Ghats lives underground nearly all year. They come up for a few days in the first monsoon rains to breed.
explanations.art: Four small pictures: an axolotl with feathery gills, a green aphid giving birth to a tiny aphid, a clownfish in a sea anemone, and fish eggs in cracked dry mud.

agreed.text: Periodical cicadas come out together after a fixed number of years, and the crowd protects them.
agreed.evidence: Emergences have been recorded in the United States since the 1600s and are mapped brood by brood. Counts show that birds eat a small share in big emergences and nearly all cicadas in small ones.

agreed.text: Cicada nymphs count the yearly cycles of the trees they feed on.
agreed.evidence: In 2000, nymphs on peach trees that were made to flower twice in one year came out one year early.

agreed.text: Salmon return to the stream where they hatched, and they find it mainly by smell.
agreed.evidence: Tagged fish return to their home streams. Fish with plugged noses could not choose the right branch. Fish raised with a chemical in the water later followed that chemical.

agreed.text: Where a population stays steady, about two young from each pair survive to breed, however many eggs are laid.
agreed.evidence: If more survived, numbers would multiply without end. If fewer survived, the animal would die out. Counts of fish, frogs and birds over many years fit this.

agreed.text: The medusa of Turritopsis dohrnii can turn back into a polyp, and cells change kind as this happens.
agreed.evidence: It was first seen in Italy in the 1980s. It has been repeated in laboratories in Italy, Japan and other countries, and the cells have been followed under the microscope.

agreed.text: A cell that has become one kind still carries the full set of genes.
agreed.evidence: John Gurdon grew frogs from the nuclei of tadpole gut cells in 1962. Shinya Yamanaka turned skin cells back into unspecialised cells in 2006. They shared a Nobel Prize in 2012.

challenging.claim: Periodical cicadas sleep underground for seventeen years.
challenging.who: A common way of telling the story
challenging.for: We never see them in all that time, and they come out all at once, as if an alarm had rung.
challenging.against: The nymphs are awake and busy. They dig, drink from roots, grow and shed their skin four times. They even count the years by the trees' sap.
challenging.context: This card is about what a cicada nymph does during the long years underground.

challenging.claim: The immortal jellyfish can never die.
challenging.for: In the laboratory, an old or starved medusa can turn back into a polyp, again and again.
challenging.against: They can be eaten, and they can die of disease. Nobody has followed one animal through the change in the sea. The scientists who study them say 'can escape death from old age', which is a smaller claim.
challenging.context: This card is about the small jellyfish Turritopsis dohrnii, whose adult can turn back into a young polyp.

challenging.claim: Salmon die after spawning because the journey wears them out.
challenging.for: They arrive thin and battered, having eaten nothing for weeks.
challenging.against: Landlocked sockeye salmon never go to sea and make only a short trip, and they still die after spawning. The breakdown is set off by hormones, which are chemical messages inside the body. The journey alone does not cause it.
challenging.context: This card is about why Pacific salmon die within days of laying their eggs.

challenging.claim: An animal that lays a million eggs and loses nearly all of them is wasting them.
challenging.for: Almost every egg dies, so it looks like a failed plan.
challenging.against: The plan leaves about two survivors, the same as an elephant's plan. And the eggs that die are eaten. They are food for small fish, crabs and other animals, so nothing leaves the sea's food supply.
challenging.context: This card is about fish and other animals that lay huge numbers of eggs and give no care.

challenging.claim: Cicadas use prime numbers to hide from their predators.
challenging.who: Popular science books, following Stephen Jay Gould
challenging.for: A 13-year or 17-year cycle would rarely match any predator's cycle of 2 to 6 years. No cicada has a 12, 14, 15, 16 or 18 year cycle.
challenging.against: Nobody has found a predator with such a cycle. Other ideas explain the primes as well, such as keeping broods from mixing. Cycles also seem to jump by four years, which could give 13 and 17 by chance.
challenging.context: This card is about why periodical cicadas have cycles of 13 and 17 years.

challenging.claim: Growing old is a law of nature for every animal.
challenging.who: Common sense for most of history
challenging.for: Every animal we know well grows old: dogs, cows, crows and people.
challenging.against: Hydra showed no ageing in a four-year study. The medusa of Turritopsis dohrnii can become young again. Some scientists still expect that all animals age, only very slowly in a few.
challenging.context: This card is about senescence, the wearing down of a body with age.

big_questions.q: A cicada lives underground for 17 years and in the air for 4 weeks. Which one is the real cicada?
big_questions.hint: Look at your Life Bars drawing. Why do we call the winged stage the 'real' one?

big_questions.q: A polyp grows from an old medusa and has the same genes. Is the polyp the same animal, or her child?
big_questions.hint: What would have to stay the same for you to call it the same animal? The body? The genes? The memories?

big_questions.q: Suppose you could become a baby again, but you would lose every memory. Would you be living longer?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you would want to keep.

big_questions.q: Birds eat thousands of cicadas so that millions can live. For one cicada who is eaten, is the plan a good one?
big_questions.hint: Nobody made the plan. Does that change your answer?

big_questions.q: A salmon spends her whole body on her eggs. Can science say what a life is for?
big_questions.hint: Science can say what leaves more young. Is that the same as what a life is for?

big_questions.q: Humans care for a child for about fifteen years. What does such a long childhood make possible?
big_questions.hint: Think about everything you have learned that you were not born knowing.

story.title: The Ones Who Came Early
story.note: A made-up story. The cicada is real. A periodical cicada lives in the Ri-Bhoi district of Meghalaya, comes out every four years in the same years as the football World Cup, and is called niangtaser by local people, who gather them to eat. Ibahun, Kyrshan, Kong Rilin, the school, the birds and the events of these evenings are imagined. The way the nymphs climb, split their skins and are eaten when few is how periodical cicadas are known to behave.
text: In Ibahun's village in the Ri-Bhoi hills, people counted some things in fours. There were four years between one football World Cup and the next. There were also four years between one coming of the niangtaser and the next, and the two always fell in the same year.
Ibahun was nine. The last time, she had been five. She remembered a torch, her mother's hand, and a noise in the trees like rain on a tin roof. That was all.

This April everybody talked about it. Her cousin Kyrshan cleaned out an old biscuit tin. "I'll fill this in one night," he said. "Fried, with salt and chilli." Kong Rilin, who sold vegetables at the Nongpoh market and knew the forest better than anyone, only said, "Not yet. The ground is still cold."
Ibahun did not want to wait for everybody. She wanted to see the first one. So each evening she took her small torch to the big trees behind the school and looked at the ground.

On the fourth evening she found a hole, as round as if someone had pushed a finger into the mud. Beside the hole a brown creature was walking slowly towards the nearest trunk. They had bent front legs like little spades, and no wings at all. A nymph. Four years ago an egg had hatched on a twig above this spot. This small animal had dropped to the ground, dug down, and lived in the dark on root sap ever since. They had been down there since Ibahun was five.

She sat on a root and watched. The nymph climbed as high as her knee and held on. For a long time nothing happened. Then the brown skin split down the back, and a pale body pushed out, as soft as wet paper. The wings came out crumpled and slowly spread flat. The whole change took almost an hour. Ibahun forgot about dinner.
"Stay there," she whispered. "I'll come back in the morning."
In the morning the empty skin was still gripping the bark. The cicada was gone. A drongo sat on the school fence, wiping his beak on the wire.
The next evening three came up. She watched all three climb. By breakfast there were three more empty skins, and the hens were scratching about under the trees, looking pleased.
Ibahun went to find Kong Rilin, who was tying mustard leaves into bundles on her veranda.

"They're all being eaten," Ibahun said. "Four years under the ground, then one night, then a bird. Four came out and four are gone. Maybe there aren't many left this year. Maybe the new road killed them."
Kong Rilin went on tying. "How many birds are there behind the school?"
"I don't know. The drongo. Some mynas. The hens."
"And how many can a drongo eat before he is full?"
Ibahun thought. "Ten? Twenty?"
"Then wait for the warm rain," said Kong Rilin, "and count again."
The warm rain came on a Thursday. It fell all afternoon, and the evening was so mild that the windows were left open. After dark Kyrshan banged on the door with his tin. "Now!" he shouted.

Behind the school the ground looked like a sieve. There were holes everywhere, and from every hole a nymph was walking to a tree. They climbed over roots, over each other, over Ibahun's sandals. The trunks were brown with them as high as she could reach. Half the village was there with torches and tins and plastic bags. People picked nymphs off the bark like berries. Kyrshan filled his tin in a quarter of an hour and ran home for another.

Ibahun did not pick any. She walked from tree to tree with her torch. On every trunk the skins were splitting, and pale new cicadas were hanging out to dry. There were hundreds and hundreds, more than she could have counted if she had counted all night.

At sunrise she came back. The drongo was there, and so were the mynas, the hens and two dogs. They had all eaten. The drongo sat on the fence with his feathers puffed out. A cicada flew past his head, slow and clumsy, and he did not even turn to look. The hens had stopped scratching. And still every tree was covered.
By the end of the week the males had begun to sing. It was the sound she remembered, like rain on a tin roof, though the sky was clear.

She thought about her first cicada, the one she had told to stay. That one had waited four years, and found the tree, and climbed well. They had done everything right except one thing. They had come up on an evening when the drongo had nobody else to choose.
Kyrshan's family ate fried niangtaser for three days. So did most of the village. It made no difference that anyone could see.

A few weeks later the trees were quiet again. Under the big tree Ibahun found a fallen twig with a row of small slits cut along it. She knew what was inside. She looked at the ground below, where the new ones would soon dig in.
She did the sum on her fingers. Next time she would be thirteen. The time after that, seventeen. She put the twig back where she had found it.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the first cicada did nothing wrong except come up alone. A drongo can eat only so many insects in a morning. When four cicadas come up, the birds eat all four. When many thousands come up on the same night, the birds, the hens, the dogs and the villagers all eat until they are full, and almost every cicada is still left. Each cicada's safety comes from the timing they share with all the others. Scientists call this predator satiation. It is the reason the nymphs wait for the same warm evening.
ask: Four cicadas came up early and all four were eaten. Thousands came up later and most lived. What was different?
Kong Rilin asked how many insects a drongo can eat before he is full. Why did that question matter?
The villagers filled tins and bags with cicadas. Why did it make no difference to the cicadas as a whole?
What signal do you think the nymphs were all waiting for?
Where else do animals arrive in a crowd? Think of winged termites after rain, or turtles on a beach.

A brown wingless cicada nymph gripping tree bark at knee height, with the skin split down the back and a pale soft cicada pulling out.
An empty brown cicada skin on a tree trunk in morning light, and a black drongo on a wire fence wiping his beak.

Night under the trees: the ground full of small holes, tree trunks covered in climbing nymphs, villagers with torches, tins and bags.
Sunrise: a drongo with puffed feathers on a fence ignoring a cicada flying past, and tree trunks still covered in cicadas.
A girl holding a fallen twig with a row of small slits, looking down at the ground under a big tree.

games.title: Whose Life Is This?
games.context: This is a card game about strange life cycles. To breed is to have babies. Each card gives three clues about one animal's life. You try to name the animal from as few clues as you can.

printables.title: 20 clue cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: Clue 1: I drink sap from tree roots, underground, for 17 years. Clue 2: Millions of us come up in the same few evenings. Clue 3: As a winged adult I live about a month.
items.b: A 17-year periodical cicada. The crowd is her protection, because predators cannot eat them all.

items.f: Clue 1: I live in the hills of Meghalaya. Clue 2: My whole population comes up together once in four years. Clue 3: People say I come in the years of the football World Cup.
items.b: The Ri-Bhoi cicada of Meghalaya, the only periodical cicada known in India.

items.f: Clue 1: I live about a year under the water of a stream. Clue 2: As a winged adult I have no working mouth. Clue 3: My adult life lasts a day or two.
items.b: A mayfly. The adult's only tasks are to mate and lay eggs.

items.f: Clue 1: I hatch in river gravel and grow up in the sea. Clue 2: I find my home stream by smell. Clue 3: I spawn once, and then I die.
items.b: A Pacific salmon, such as a sockeye. Her body then feeds the river and the forest.

items.f: Clue 1: I live in the Bay of Bengal. Clue 2: In the monsoon I swim up the Godavari or the Hooghly to spawn. Clue 3: Unlike a Pacific salmon, I may live to spawn again.
items.b: A hilsa. In Andhra Pradesh the river-run hilsa is called pulasa.

items.f: Clue 1: I am about 4 millimetres wide and live in the sea. Clue 2: My young stage is a polyp fixed to a rock. Clue 3: When I am old or starved, I can turn back into a polyp.
items.b: The immortal jellyfish, Turritopsis dohrnii. Her cells change from one kind into another.

items.f: Clue 1: I have eight arms and live in the cold sea. Clue 2: I guard my eggs for about six months and eat nothing. Clue 3: I die around the time my eggs hatch.
items.b: A female giant Pacific octopus. She breeds only once.

items.f: Clue 1: I am one of the heaviest fish with a bony skeleton. Clue 2: One of us was found carrying about 300 million eggs. Clue 3: I give my eggs no care at all.
items.b: An ocean sunfish. Each egg is tiny, and almost every one is eaten.

items.f: Clue 1: I am a bird who cannot fly, from New Zealand. Clue 2: I lay one egg at a time. Clue 3: My egg weighs about a fifth as much as I do.
items.b: A kiwi. One huge egg gives a chick who can feed themself within days.

items.f: Clue 1: I am a fly from Africa. Clue 2: I have one baby at a time, and the baby grows inside me. Clue 3: I feed my baby on a liquid like milk.
items.b: A tsetse fly. Not every insect lays many eggs.

items.f: Clue 1: I am a salamander from lakes near Mexico City. Clue 2: I keep my feathery gills all my life. Clue 3: I breed while my body still looks young.
items.b: An axolotl. She becomes a parent without ever changing into the land form.

items.f: Clue 1: I am a small insect who sucks sap from young leaves. Clue 2: In warm months I give birth to live daughters, with no father. Clue 3: My daughter can carry her own daughters before she is born.
items.b: An aphid. One mother can become a crowd in two weeks.

items.f: Clue 1: I come ashore in Odisha with thousands of others on the same nights. Clue 2: I bury about a hundred eggs in the sand and go back to sea. Clue 3: My young hatch with no parent near.
items.b: An olive ridley turtle. So many nests are dug at once that predators cannot find them all.

items.f: Clue 1: I am the largest land animal in India. Clue 2: My mother carried me for about 22 months. Clue 3: I drink milk for two years or more, and my herd guards me.
items.b: An Asian elephant. Few young, and years of care for each one.

items.f: Clue 1: I live in your kitchen, in a jar of whole moong or cowpea. Clue 2: My mother glued her egg onto one seed, and I grew up inside that seed. Clue 3: As an adult I need no food, and I live about ten days.
items.b: A pulse beetle. The round hole in the seed is the door the adult cut to get out.

items.f: Clue 1: I am a small fish who lives in a pool that dries up every year. Clue 2: I grow up and breed within a few weeks. Clue 3: My eggs wait in the dry mud for months until the rain comes back.
items.b: An annual killifish. The eggs carry the animal through the dry season.

items.f: Clue 1: I live among the tentacles of a sea anemone. Clue 2: Every one of us begins adult life as a male. Clue 3: When the female of my group dies, the biggest male becomes the female.
items.b: A clownfish. The same fish is a father first and a mother later.

items.f: Clue 1: I grow up in Indian rivers and ponds for many years. Clue 2: Then I swim down to the sea, the opposite of a salmon. Clue 3: I spawn once in the deep sea, and I die there.
items.b: An Indian mottled eel. Her young drift back to the rivers.

items.f: Clue 1: I live underground in the Western Ghats nearly all year. Clue 2: I come up for a few days when the first monsoon rain falls. Clue 3: My tadpoles cling to rocks in fast streams with sucker mouths.
items.b: A purple frog, named by scientists only in 2003.

items.f: Clue 1: My young are helpless at birth. Clue 2: I care for each child for about fifteen years. Clue 3: I often live for decades after my last child is born.
items.b: A human. Our long childhood is spent learning from others.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, clue side up. Do not look at the backs.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads out Clue 1 only.
The other players may each make one guess. A right guess after Clue 1 scores 3 points.
If nobody is right, the reader reads Clue 2. A right guess now scores 2 points. After Clue 3 a right guess scores 1 point.
The reader turns the card over and reads the back aloud. Then the next player becomes the reader.
After 20 cards, the player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: cover Clues 2 and 3 with your hand and score yourself the same way. Try to reach 30 points, then play again another day to beat your score.

setup.art: A child reading one clue aloud from a card while another child thinks with a finger on her chin.
setup.caption: 2. Read one clue at a time. Each player may guess once after every clue.

setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over, read the back and write the points.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards. 2. Shuffle them. 3. Put them in a pile, clue side up. 4. Take a paper and a pencil for the scores.
flow.say: Each card describes one animal's life in three clues. The first clue is the hardest. Let's see how few clues we need.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Put them in a pile with the clues facing up.
flow.context: This is the first step of Whose Life Is This? Here you get the clue cards ready.

flow.do: 1. Read Clue 1 of the top card. 2. Let each player guess once. 3. If nobody is right, read Clue 2, and then Clue 3. 4. Turn the card and read the back. 5. Write the points and pass the pile to the next reader.
flow.say: Listen to the clue. Which animals could it be? What would you need to know to be sure?
flow.kid: Read one clue. Guess the animal. If you are wrong, read the next clue.

ask.q: A clue says the animal breeds once and then dies. Which animals could that be?
good: A Pacific salmon, a mayfly, an octopus, an eel or a periodical cicada.
We need another clue to choose between them.

flow.parent: A wrong guess is useful. Ask which clue would tell the two animals apart. If a card is new to your child, read all three clues and the back, and put the card back in the pile to meet again.
flow.context: This is the main part of Whose Life Is This? Here you guess each animal from as few clues as you can.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Spread all 20 cards out, answer side up. 3. Sort them into two heaps: animals who breed once, and animals who breed many times.
flow.say: Which animal surprised you most? Now let's sort them. Who breeds once in a life, and who breeds many times?
flow.kid: Count your points. Then sort the cards. Who breeds once? Who breeds many times?
flow.parent: Breed once: both cicadas, the mayfly, the Pacific salmon, the octopus, the eel and the pulse beetle. The killifish is a fair argument either way, because they breed for several weeks in their one short season. All the others breed many times.

check.q: Which of these animals breeds only once in her life?
check.why: A female giant Pacific octopus lays one batch of eggs, guards them for months and dies. A hilsa may spawn again in a later year, and an elephant has several calves. Choosing the hilsa usually means mixing her up with the Pacific salmon, who does die after spawning.

flow.context: This is the last step of Whose Life Is This? Here you count the points and sort the animals by how often they breed.

games.title: Emerge! Choose your year
games.context: This is a game for 2 to 4 players about when to come out of the ground. Each player is a brood of ten cicadas and secretly chooses a year from 12 to 18. Birds eat more in some years than in others. The game uses one idea about prime numbers, and scientists do not agree that the idea is right.

printables.title: 28 year chits to cut out: one set of seven for each player
The birds' meal chart
items: Year 12: the birds eat 6 (every year 2, plus 2 for an even year, plus 2 for a multiple of 3)
Year 14: the birds eat 4 (an even year)
Year 15: the birds eat 4 (a multiple of 3)
Year 16: the birds eat 4 (an even year)
Year 18: the birds eat 6 (an even year and a multiple of 3)

printables.title: Score sheet for six rounds
items: Round 1: year chosen ____  cicadas left out of 10 ____
Round 2: year chosen ____  cicadas left out of 10 ____
Round 3: year chosen ____  cicadas left out of 10 ____
Round 4: year chosen ____  cicadas left out of 10 ____
Round 5: year chosen ____  cicadas left out of 10 ____
Round 6: year chosen ____  cicadas left out of 10 ____
Total cicadas left after six rounds ____

rules: Each player takes ten rajma or chana as cicadas, and one set of seven year chits.
In each round, every player secretly chooses one year chit and lays it face down. Do not talk about your choice.
Turn all the chits over together.

Look up each chosen year on the birds' meal chart. The birds eat 2 cicadas in any year. They eat 2 more in an even year, because one predator has a good year every 2 years. They eat 2 more in a year that 3 divides exactly, because another predator has a good year every 3 years.
Players who chose the same year share that year's meal. They take turns to give up one cicada each, youngest first, until the meal is eaten.
Write down how many cicadas you have left. Then take all ten back for the next round.
Play six rounds. The player with the highest total wins.

setup.art: Two players at a table, each with a small heap of ten rajma and a fan of seven paper chits numbered 12 to 18.
setup.caption: 1. Each player takes ten rajma and seven year chits.

setup.art: Two paper chits lying face down on the table between the two players.
setup.caption: 2. Secretly choose a year and lay the chit face down.

setup.caption: 3. Turn the chits over. Read the birds' meal from the chart and share it.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the year chits, the meal chart and the score sheet. 2. Give each player ten rajma and seven chits. 3. Read the rules aloud once.
flow.say: You are a brood of ten cicadas. You must choose how many years to stay underground. Some years are more dangerous than others.
flow.kid: Take ten rajma and seven chits. You are a brood of cicadas.
flow.context: This is the first step of Emerge! Here you set up the chits, the meal chart and the cicadas.

flow.do: 1. Play six rounds by the rules. 2. After each round, every player writes the year they chose and the cicadas they have left. 3. Do not explain the pattern. Let your child find it.
flow.say: Choose your year. Turn over. How many do the birds eat this year? Who shares that meal?
flow.kid: Choose a year. Turn your chit over. Read the birds' meal. Share it. Write what you have left.

ask.q: Which years cost you the most cicadas? What do those numbers have in common?
good: 12 and 18 cost the most.
Both can be divided by 2 and by 3.

ask.q: What happened when we both chose the same year?
good: We shared one meal, so each of us lost fewer.

flow.parent: Most children find by round three or four that 13 and 17 are the cheap years. The second discovery is slower. Two broods in the same year share one meal, so they lose fewer each. If your child has not noticed, play 13 yourself twice running and say nothing.
flow.context: This is the main part of Emerge! Here you play six rounds and write down the scores.

flow.do: 1. Add up the scores. 2. Ask which years were safest and why. 3. Ask what 13 and 17 have that 12 and 18 lack. 4. Read the note in the parent box aloud.
flow.say: Which years were safest? What is special about 13 and 17? And was it better to come out alone or in the same year as the other brood?
flow.kid: Add up your scores. Which years were safest? Why? Was it better to share a year?
flow.parent: Say this to your child afterwards. Real periodical cicadas do have 13-year and 17-year cycles. But nobody has found predators with 2-year and 3-year cycles. So this game shows one idea that scientists argue about. The part about sharing a year is well tested.

check.q: In Emerge!, why is 13 a safer year than 12?
check.why: The game's two predators have good years every 2 years and every 3 years. Year 12 falls on both, and year 13 falls on neither, because 13 is a prime number. Choosing 'a bigger number' forgets that 14, 15, 16 and 18 are bigger still and less safe.

flow.context: This is the last step of Emerge! Here you add up the scores and talk about the safest years.

experiments.title: The Crowd Test: is it safer to come out alone or all together?
experiments.context: In this experiment, rajma on a towel are cicadas coming out of the ground. One person is a hungry bird who picks them up for ten seconds. You will find out if a cicada is safer coming out alone or in a big crowd.
experiments.question: Sixty cicadas must come out of the ground. Do more of them live if ten come out on each of six evenings, or if all sixty come out on one evening? And how does the number a bird eats change as the crowd gets bigger?
experiments.predict: Guess first. With which plan will more cicadas be left alive: ten each evening for six evenings, or all sixty on one evening? About how many will be left each time? Then guess again. If the crowd is twice as big, will the bird eat twice as many? Write both guesses and your reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the size of the crowd. Keep the same bird, who uses the same hand and picks up one rajma at a time. Keep the same towel and the same ten seconds. The bird closes their eyes while the rajma are scattered, so they cannot plan. Plan A is six short goes. Do Plan B three times and find the mean, because one go can be a fluke.

materials.item: dry rajma or kabuli chana
a bath towel, spread flat on the floor or a table
a steel tumbler
a phone timer or a clock with a seconds hand
a notebook, a pencil and a ruler

schedule.what: Test ten at a time against sixty at once. Then test crowds of 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80. Fill in the table and draw a line graph.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for Plan A, Plan B and the five crowd sizes. Draw a line graph with the crowd size along the bottom and the number eaten up the side. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: rajma eaten in ten seconds
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished graph can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A bath towel spread flat on the floor, a plate of rajma, a steel tumbler beside the towel and a phone showing a timer.
setup.caption: 1. Spread the towel flat. Put the tumbler beside it.

setup.art: A child with eyes closed kneeling by the towel while a grown-up scatters ten rajma all over the towel.
setup.caption: 2. The bird closes their eyes. The other person scatters the rajma.

setup.art: The child picking up one rajma with one hand and dropping it into the tumbler, while the grown-up watches the timer.
setup.caption: 3. For ten seconds the bird picks up one at a time and drops each into the tumbler.

setup.art: A notebook table with rows for crowd sizes 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80, and columns for eaten and left.
setup.caption: 4. Count the rajma in the tumbler and write the number down.

flow.do: 1. Spread the towel flat on the floor or a table. 2. Count 100 rajma onto a plate. 3. Stand the tumbler beside the towel. 4. Agree the picking rule: one hand, one rajma at a time, and each one goes into the tumbler before the next. 5. Let the bird practise for five seconds.
flow.say: These rajma are cicadas coming out of the ground. You are a hungry bird. You may pick up only one at a time, with one hand.
flow.kid: Spread the towel flat. Count 100 rajma. You are the bird. Pick up one at a time.
flow.parent: The test needs two people: the bird, and someone to scatter and to time. Use the whole towel, so that the bird has to reach.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Crowd Test. Here you set up the towel, the rajma and the picking rule.

flow.do: 1. Read out the two plans. 2. Ask for the first guess, with numbers, and the reason. 3. Ask the second guess, about a crowd twice as big. 4. Write both down.
flow.say: Ten each evening for six evenings, or all sixty on one evening. Which plan leaves more cicadas alive, and how many? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which plan saves more cicadas, and how many are left. Write your guess down.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: The bird has the same time each evening, so more evenings means more eaten.
In a big crowd the bird cannot get to everyone.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children expect the plans to come out about equal, because the same sixty cicadas come out either way.
flow.context: This step of the Crowd Test is for guessing. You guess before any rajma go on the towel.

flow.do: 1. Plan A. The bird closes their eyes. 2. Scatter 10 rajma all over the towel. 3. Say 'go' and time 10 seconds, then say 'stop'. 4. Count the rajma in the tumbler and write the number eaten. 5. Clear the towel and empty the tumbler. 6. Do this six times, for six evenings. 7. Add up how many were left over the six evenings.
flow.say: This is Plan A. Ten cicadas come out each evening. You have ten seconds each evening. Close your eyes while I scatter them.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Open them on 'go'. Pick up rajma for ten seconds. Count what you ate. Do six evenings.
flow.parent: Expect the bird to get six to nine of the ten each evening. If the bird gets all ten every time, use a bigger towel or cut the time to seven seconds, and keep that time for the whole test.
flow.context: This is Plan A of the Crowd Test. Here ten rajma come out on each of six evenings, and the bird picks for ten seconds each time.

flow.do: 1. Plan B. The bird closes their eyes. 2. Scatter 60 rajma all over the towel. 3. Time 10 seconds. 4. Count the rajma in the tumbler. Take that number from 60 to find how many were left. 5. Do Plan B three times. 6. Add the three numbers left and divide by 3 to find the mean.
flow.say: This is Plan B. All sixty come out on one evening. You still have only ten seconds. Then no more cicadas come out on the other five evenings.
flow.kid: Now sixty come out at once. Pick for ten seconds. Count what you ate. Do this three times.
flow.context: This is Plan B of the Crowd Test. Here all sixty rajma come out on one evening, and the bird picks for ten seconds.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what will happen with crowds of 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80. 2. Test each crowd size once, for 10 seconds. 3. Write the number eaten and the number left each time.
flow.say: Now we change the crowd size step by step. Each crowd is twice as big as the one before. Will you eat twice as many each time?
flow.kid: Test crowds of 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80. Ten seconds each. Write what you ate each time.

ask.q: What do you expect to eat from a crowd of 80, and why?
good: About the same as from 40, because I cannot pick any faster.
A few more, because they are closer together.

flow.context: This is part 2 of the Crowd Test. Here the bird picks from crowds of five different sizes.

flow.do: 1. For each row, write the share eaten as a fraction, such as 8 out of 10. 2. Draw a line graph, or build a bar of rajma for each crowd size. Put the crowd size along the bottom and the number eaten up the side. 3. Look at the shape of the line.
flow.say: Let's write each result as a share. Eight out of ten is a big share. Nine out of eighty is a small share. Now draw the graph.
flow.kid: Write each result as a share, like 8 out of 10. Draw the line graph. What shape is the line?
flow.parent: The line usually climbs at first and then goes nearly flat. If one point is far off the others, test that crowd size again and say so in the table.
flow.context: This step of the Crowd Test is for the shares and the line graph.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for the three sentences. 2. Ask what is different for real cicadas and real birds. 3. Only then read the card 'Safety in a crowd' together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Then tell me one thing our test leaves out about real birds.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why. What does our test leave out?

ask.q: The bird ate about the same number from 40 as from 80. So what happened to each cicada's chance of being eaten?
good: It halved, because the same meal was shared among twice as many.
The bigger the crowd, the safer each one is.

ask.q: What does our test leave out about real birds and cicadas?
good: Real birds get full, and that also limits them.
More birds may fly in when they see a crowd.
Real cicadas can fly away or hide.

flow.parent: A model shows one idea clearly and leaves other things out. Here the bird is limited by time. Real birds are limited by time and by a full stomach. Both limits give the same result: a predator can eat only so many.

check.q: In the Crowd Test, a bird ate 8 rajma from a crowd of 10 and 9 from a crowd of 80. What does this show?
options: A bigger crowd makes the bird hungrier
Each one is much safer in the bigger crowd
The bird cannot see a big crowd
check.why: The bird ate almost the same number each time, so the share eaten fell from 8 in 10 to 9 in 80. Each member of the big crowd had a much smaller chance of being picked. Choosing 'hungrier' usually means looking at the number eaten and missing the share.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Crowd Test. Here you explain your results and say what the model leaves out.

experiments.title: The Home Stream Test: how weak a smell can your nose follow?
experiments.context: A salmon finds her home stream by a smell that is very weak by the time it reaches the river mouth. In this experiment you mix a kitchen smell with more and more water. Then you find the weakest mixture your nose can still pick out from plain water.
experiments.question: How much water can be added to a smell before your nose can no longer tell it from plain water?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which is the weakest mixture you will still be able to pick out: 1 part in 10, 1 in 100, 1 in 1,000 or 1 in 10,000? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the strength of the mixture. Use three katoris of the same kind, with the same amount of liquid in each. The child must not see the katoris being filled. The grown-up looks away while the child chooses, so that a glance cannot give the answer. Do three tries at each strength, because one right pick out of three katoris can be luck.

materials.item: a liquid with a strong smell: vanilla essence, rose water or white vinegar
small steel katoris or cups of the same kind, for the tests
any other small cups or tumblers, for the four mixtures
a teaspoon, and a jug of drinking water
small slips of paper, a pencil and a notebook

experiments.safety: Smell the mixtures and do not drink them. Vanilla essence contains alcohol.

schedule.what: Make four mixtures, each ten times weaker than the one before. Test each one three times against plain water. Find the weakest that the nose can pick out.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with a tick or a cross for every try. Circle the weakest strength where you got 3 out of 3. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think a nose has a limit.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: right picks out of 3 tries
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Four cups in a row on paper slips labelled 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000, with a teaspoon carrying liquid from the first cup to the second.
setup.caption: 1. Make four mixtures. Each is ten times weaker than the one before.

setup.art: Three matching steel katoris in a row, each holding a little clear liquid, with a child's back turned while a grown-up fills them.
setup.caption: 2. Out of sight, put a mixture in one katori and plain water in two.

setup.art: A child bending to sniff the middle one of three katoris while the grown-up looks away.
setup.caption: 3. Smell all three and pick the home stream. Do three tries at each strength.

flow.do: 1. Write 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 on four paper slips and stand a cup on each. 2. Put 9 teaspoons of water into each cup. 3. Add 1 teaspoon of the smelly liquid to cup 10 and stir. 4. Rinse the spoon. Move 1 teaspoon from cup 10 into cup 100 and stir. 5. Rinse the spoon. Move 1 teaspoon from cup 100 into cup 1,000. 6. Rinse again. Move 1 teaspoon from cup 1,000 into cup 10,000.
flow.say: Each cup is ten times weaker than the one before. Cup 10 has one part of smell in ten parts. Cup 10,000 has one part in ten thousand.
flow.kid: Put 9 spoons of water in each cup. Add 1 spoon of smell to the first. Then pass 1 spoon along the row.
flow.parent: Rinsing the spoon matters. A spoon that has been in a strong cup carries smell into the weak ones.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Home Stream Test. Here you make four mixtures, each ten times weaker than the last.

flow.do: 1. Let your child smell cup 10 for a few breaths. 2. Tell them this is the smell of their home stream. 3. Ask for their guess and the reason. 4. Write it down.
flow.say: This is the smell of your home stream. Learn it well. How weak can it get before your nose loses it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Smell the first cup. This is your home stream. Guess the weakest cup you can still smell.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Ten thousand is a lot of water for one spoon of smell.
I can smell food from far away, so maybe my nose is good.

flow.context: This step of the Home Stream Test is for learning the smell and guessing. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Start with the weakest, cup 10,000. Your child turns away. 2. Put 3 teaspoons of the mixture into one katori and 3 teaspoons of plain water into each of the other two. 3. Shuffle the katoris, and remember where the mixture is. 4. Look away while your child smells all three and picks one. 5. Write a tick or a cross. 6. Shuffle and try again, until you have three tries. 7. Rinse the katoris. Do the same for cups 1,000, 100 and 10.
flow.say: Three streams meet here. One is your home stream. Smell each one and choose. Do not taste. I will look away while you choose.
flow.kid: Turn away. Then smell all three katoris. Pick your home stream. Do three tries at each strength.
flow.parent: We go from weakest to strongest, because a strong smell tires the nose for a while. Between tries, your child takes two breaths of fresh air. If they get 3 out of 3 at cup 10,000, make a cup 100,000 and test that too. If they get none even at cup 10, start again with a stronger liquid.
flow.context: This is the main step of the Home Stream Test. Here you try to pick out each mixture from two katoris of plain water.

flow.do: 1. Count the right picks at each strength. 2. Circle the weakest strength with 3 out of 3. 3. Ask how many right picks pure guessing would give.
flow.say: Where did your nose lose the stream? If you only guessed, how many of three tries would you expect to get right?
flow.kid: Count your right picks. Circle the weakest cup with 3 out of 3. Could that be luck?

ask.q: If you only guessed, how often would you be right?
good: About one time in three, because there are three katoris.
Getting all three right by luck is rare, about 1 time in 27.

flow.context: This step of the Home Stream Test is for the results table. You find the weakest mixture your nose could pick out.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for the three sentences. 2. Ask how a salmon's task is like this test, and how it differs. 3. Only then read the card 'How a salmon finds home' together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why a nose has a limit. Then tell me how a salmon's task is like yours.
flow.kid: Say what you guessed. Say what you found. Say why a nose has a limit. How is a salmon's task like yours?

ask.q: How is a salmon's task like this test?
good: She learns one smell when she is young.
At each fork in the river she picks the branch with that smell.
The smell gets weaker the further she is from home.

flow.parent: A smell is made of tiny particles that reach cells in the nose. With enough water there are too few particles for the nose to notice. A salmon's nose notices smells many thousands of times weaker than ours can.

check.q: A girl picks the home katori right in 1 try out of 3. What is the best conclusion?
options: She can smell that strength well
She was probably guessing at that strength
check.why: With three katoris, pure guessing is right about one time in three. So 1 out of 3 is what guessing gives. Only 3 out of 3 is good evidence that the nose found the smell. Choosing the first answer usually means counting one right pick as proof.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Home Stream Test. Here you explain your results and compare your nose with a salmon's.

activities.title: Life Bars: how much of a life is spent growing up?
activities.context: In this activity you make the lives of five animals as paper strips of the same length. On each strip you colour the part of life spent as a youngster, before the body is able to have young. You will find out how much of their lives the five animals spend growing up.

materials.item: a sheet of paper, a ruler and a pencil
a colour pencil or crayon

activities.record: Keep the strips. On a paper beside them write one sentence: which animal spends the biggest share of life as a youngster, and which the smallest.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with five empty bars, each 20 centimetres long, labelled human, elephant, hen, cicada and mayfly.
setup.caption: 1. Cut five strips, each 20 centimetres long. Each strip is one whole life.

setup.art: The same five bars with the first part of each shaded: a short shaded part for the hen, longer for the human and elephant, and almost the whole bar for the cicada and mayfly.
setup.caption: 2. Shade the part of each life spent as a youngster.

setup.art: A child pointing with a pencil tip at the tiny unshaded end of the cicada's bar.
setup.caption: 3. Look at what is left for adult life.

flow.do: 1. Name the five animals: a human, an Asian elephant, a hen, a 17-year cicada and a mayfly. 2. Ask which one spends the biggest share of life as a youngster, and why. 3. Write the guess down.
flow.say: A youngster here means an animal whose body cannot yet have young. Which of these five spends the biggest share of life like that? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which animal spends the biggest share of life as a youngster? Guess. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Life Bars. Here you guess which animal spends the biggest share of life growing up.

flow.do: 1. Cut five paper strips, each 20 centimetres long and 1 centimetre wide. 2. Lay them in a row with a gap between them. 3. Write one animal's name on each strip.
flow.say: Each strip is one whole life, from the start to the end. The lives are different lengths, but we cut every strip the same length. Then we can compare the shares.
