flow.kid: Cut five strips. Make each one 20 cm long. Write an animal's name on each strip.
flow.context: This step of Life Bars is for drawing five bars of the same length, one for each animal's whole life.

flow.do: 1. A human lives about 70 years, and the body can have children from about 14. Ask what fraction 14 is of 70, and how many centimetres of the bar that is. 2. Shade that part. 3. An elephant lives about 60 years and can have her first calf at about 15. Work out and shade her bar.
flow.say: Fourteen years out of seventy. What fraction is that? How many centimetres of a 20 centimetre bar? Now do the elephant: fifteen out of sixty.
flow.kid: Human: 14 years out of 70. What fraction? Shade it. Elephant: 15 out of 60. Shade it.
flow.parent: 14 out of 70 is one fifth, and a fifth of 20 centimetres is 4 centimetres. 15 out of 60 is one quarter, which is 5 centimetres. A human body can have children from about 14, at a stage called puberty. People wisely wait many more years.
flow.context: This step of Life Bars is for working out and shading the human's bar and the elephant's bar.

flow.do: 1. A hen can lay at 5 months and lives about 6 years. Shade 1.4 centimetres of her bar. 2. A periodical cicada is a nymph for 17 years and an adult for about 4 weeks. Shade all of the bar but the last 1 millimetre. 3. A mayfly is a nymph for about a year and an adult for a day. Shade the whole bar, and leave one thin pencil line at the end for the adult.
flow.say: A nymph is a young insect that is not yet an adult. For the last three I will read you the lengths. The hen is 1.4 centimetres. The cicada is everything except the last millimetre. The mayfly is everything except one pencil line.
flow.kid: Hen: shade 1.4 cm. Cicada: shade all but 1 mm. Mayfly: shade all but one thin line.
flow.context: This step of Life Bars is for shading the bars of the hen, the cicada and the mayfly.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to put the animals in order, from the smallest share of life as a youngster to the biggest. 2. Compare with the guess. 3. Ask how they would show the strip of a jellyfish who can turn from adult back to young.
flow.say: Put them in order. Was your guess right? Now, one small jellyfish can turn from an adult back into a youngster. How would you show her strip?
flow.kid: Put the animals in order. Was your guess right? How would you show a jellyfish who turns young again?

ask.q: Which stage is most of a cicada's life: the young nymph or the winged adult?
good: The nymph, for nearly all of the 17 years.
The winged stage is only the last month.

flow.parent: There is no right way to draw the jellyfish. A bar that loops back on itself is a good answer. So is 'I cannot, because there is no end to measure to'.

check.q: A periodical cicada lives 17 years. About how long is the winged adult stage?
check.why: The nymph lives underground for 17 years, and the winged adult lives about four weeks. Choosing 8 or 16 years usually comes from expecting adult life to be the long part, as it is for humans.

flow.context: This is the last step of Life Bars. Here you compare the five bars and think about an animal whose bar cannot be drawn.

activities.title: Run It Backwards: a dough model of the immortal jellyfish
activities.context: One small jellyfish can turn from a swimming adult, called a medusa, back into a young polyp fixed to a rock. In this activity you build a medusa from dough and turn her into a polyp without adding or removing any dough. Then you say what the model leaves out.

materials.item: atta dough or play clay, a ball the size of a lemon
a plate, and a toothpick or a matchstick
paper and a pencil

activities.record: Draw the jellyfish life cycle as a circle of stages: egg, swimming larva, polyp, young medusa, adult medusa. Then add one more arrow, from the adult medusa back to the polyp. You can draw it, or tell it to your grown-up. Write one thing the dough model shows well and one thing it leaves out.

setup.art: A dough jellyfish on a plate: a bowl-shaped bell upside down, eight thin tentacles around the rim and a short mouth tube in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Build a medusa: a bell, eight tentacles and a mouth tube.

setup.art: The same dough squashed into a smooth ball on the plate.
setup.caption: 2. Fold everything in and roll a ball. Add nothing and take nothing away.

setup.art: The dough reshaped into a short stalk stuck to the plate with small tentacles on top, and two tiny dough jellyfish pinched off beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Shape the ball into a polyp. Then pinch off small new medusae.

flow.do: 1. Take two thirds of the dough and shape a bell like a small upturned bowl. 2. Roll eight thin tentacles and press them round the rim. 3. Make a short tube and press it under the middle, as the mouth. 4. Ask what job each part does.
flow.say: This is a medusa, the adult jellyfish. What do you think the bell does? The tentacles? The tube in the middle?
flow.kid: Make a bell. Add eight tentacles. Add a mouth tube underneath. What does each part do?
flow.parent: The bell squeezes to swim. The tentacles sting and catch tiny animals. The tube is the mouth and leads to the stomach. Each job is done by its own kinds of cells.
flow.context: This is the first step of Run It Backwards. Here you build an adult jellyfish, called a medusa, from dough.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child the medusa is old and has no food. 2. Ask what she could do with the body she has. 3. After the guess, fold the tentacles into the bell and roll everything into one ball.
flow.say: She is old and starving. She has only the body she has. What could she do? Say your idea first. Then we will do what the real jellyfish does.
flow.kid: She is old and hungry. What could she do? Guess. Then fold her into a ball.
flow.context: This step of Run It Backwards turns the dough medusa into a ball, as the real jellyfish does when she is old or starved.

flow.do: 1. Press the ball onto the plate. 2. Pull part of it up into a short stalk. 3. Pinch small tentacles round the top of the stalk. This is a polyp. 4. Pinch two or three small buds off the side and shape each into a tiny medusa.
flow.say: The ball sinks and sticks to a rock. Now shape the young stage, the polyp, from the same dough. Then let the polyp bud off new little medusae.
flow.kid: Stick the ball down. Pull up a stalk. Add small tentacles. Pinch off two tiny new medusae.
flow.context: This step of Run It Backwards shapes the ball into a polyp, the young stage, and buds new small medusae from the polyp.

flow.do: 1. Ask where the material for the polyp came from. 2. Ask what the dough model leaves out. 3. Your child says the five stages in a circle (egg, swimming larva, polyp, young medusa, adult medusa) and points to the extra backward step.
flow.say: Where did the polyp's body come from? Dough has no cells. So what must happen inside the real jellyfish that our dough cannot show?
flow.kid: Where did the polyp's body come from? Then say the five stages in a circle and point to the backward step.

ask.q: What must happen inside the real jellyfish that dough cannot show?
good: The cells have to change kind, for example a muscle cell into another kind of cell.
The same genes are there, and different ones get switched on.

flow.parent: The model shows that nothing is added: the old body is the material for the new one. It leaves out the cells. In the real animal the change takes about three days, and cells switch some genes off and others on.

check.q: When the immortal jellyfish turns from a medusa into a polyp, where does the polyp's body come from?
options: From the medusa's own cells, which change kind
check.why: The medusa's own cells are reused, and many of them change from one kind into another. No egg is involved, and the medusa is often starving at the time. Choosing 'a new egg' means thinking of the usual way a polyp begins.

flow.context: This is the last step of Run It Backwards. Here you say what the dough model shows and what it leaves out.

activities.title: The Egg Budget: many small eggs or a few big ones?
activities.context: A mother animal has only so much material in her body to turn into eggs. In this activity one ball of dough is that material. You find out how many big eggs or small eggs it makes, and what each kind of egg is good for.

materials.item: atta dough or play clay, a ball about 3 centimetres across, the size of an amla
plates
one dry chana, to show the size of a small egg
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Write two numbers: how many big eggs the ball made, and how many small eggs. Then write which kind of egg you would lay if you could guard your nest, and which if your eggs drifted away in the sea, and why.

setup.art: A ball of dough the size of an amla on a plate beside a ruler showing about 3 centimetres.
setup.caption: 1. One ball of dough is all the egg material the mother has.

setup.art: A plate with four large dough eggs.
setup.caption: 2. First make four big eggs from the whole ball.

setup.art: A plate covered with about fifty tiny dough eggs, each the size of a chana, with one real chana beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Roll the dough up again. Now make eggs the size of a chana and count them.

flow.do: 1. Show the ball of dough and one chana. 2. Ask how many chana-sized eggs the ball will make, and why. 3. Ask whether a mother could have many eggs that are also big. Write the guesses.
flow.say: This ball is all the egg material one mother has. How many eggs the size of this chana will it make? Could she have many eggs and big eggs too? Why?
flow.kid: This ball is all the mother has for eggs. How many chana-sized eggs will it make? Guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Egg Budget. Here you guess how many small eggs one ball of dough will make.

flow.do: 1. Divide the whole ball into four equal eggs. 2. Put them on a plate. 3. Ask what a baby from a big egg starts life with.
flow.say: Four big eggs. Each one holds a lot of food. What does a baby from a big egg start life with?
flow.kid: Make four big eggs from the whole ball. Put them on a plate.

ask.q: What does a baby from a big egg start life with?
good: A big body and a store of food.
A better chance of living through the first days.

flow.context: This step of the Egg Budget makes four big eggs from the whole ball of dough.

flow.do: 1. Roll the four eggs back into one ball. 2. Now pinch off pieces and roll eggs the size of the chana. 3. Keep going until the dough is used up. 4. Count the eggs.
flow.say: Same ball, same mother. Now make every egg as small as this chana. Let's both roll, and then count.
flow.kid: Roll the dough into one ball again. Now make eggs as small as the chana. Count them.
flow.parent: Expect between 30 and 60 small eggs. Two people rolling together finish in about five minutes.
flow.context: This step of the Egg Budget makes as many chana-sized eggs as the same ball of dough allows.

flow.do: 1. Compare the two numbers with the guess. 2. Read out three real animals. A kiwi lays one egg, a fifth of her own weight. A hen lays one egg a day. An ocean sunfish can carry 300 million tiny eggs. 3. Ask which way suits a mother who guards her nest, and which suits a fish whose eggs drift away.
flow.say: Four big ones or about fifty small ones, from the same dough. Which way suits a mother who can guard her nest? Which suits a fish whose eggs drift away? Why?
flow.kid: Which way suits a mother who guards her nest? Which suits a fish whose eggs drift off? Why?

ask.q: Why would a fish whose eggs drift away make millions of tiny ones?
good: She cannot protect any of them, so most will be eaten whatever their size.
With millions, a few will land by luck in a safe place with food.

check.q: Why can't a fish lay 300 million eggs that are each as big as a hen's egg?
options: Her body has only so much material for eggs
Fish do not like big eggs
check.why: Eggs are made from the mother's own body and food. A fixed amount of material can be cut into a few big eggs or many small ones. Three hundred million hen-sized eggs would weigh far more than any fish.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Egg Budget. Here you match big eggs and small eggs to the lives of real animals.

activities.title: Three Survival Curves: when in life do most animals die?
activities.context: A survival curve is a line graph that shows how many animals from a starting group are still alive at each age. In this activity you draw three survival curves from a table and work out which animals each one fits.

materials.item: squared paper, or plain paper and a ruler
colour pencils
a pencil

activities.record: Keep the graph. Label each line with one real animal that fits it. Write one sentence for each line saying when in life most of those animals die.

setup.art: A hand drawing two graph axes on squared paper: the bottom line marked start, quarter, half, three quarters and end, the side line marked 0 to 100.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the axes. Along the bottom is age. Up the side is how many are still alive.

setup.art: The graph with three sets of five dots in three colours.
setup.caption: 2. Plot the five numbers for each of the three animals.

setup.art: The finished graph with three lines: one staying high then dropping, one sloping steadily down, one dropping at once to near zero.
setup.caption: 3. Join the dots and compare the three shapes.

flow.do: 1. Say that 100 elephants are born and 100 fish hatch on the same day. 2. Ask how many of each will still be alive a quarter of the way through their longest life, and why. 3. Write the guesses.
flow.say: A hundred elephant calves and a hundred newly hatched fish start life together. A quarter of the way through life, how many of each are still alive? Why?
flow.kid: 100 elephants are born. 100 fish hatch. How many of each are alive a quarter of the way through life? Guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Survival Curves. Here you guess how many young elephants and young fish stay alive.

flow.do: 1. Draw a line along the bottom, 12 centimetres long. Mark it every 3 centimetres: start, quarter, half, three quarters, end. 2. Draw a line up the side, 10 centimetres high. Mark it every centimetre: 0, 10, 20 and so on up to 100.
flow.say: Along the bottom is age, as a share of the longest life. Up the side is how many of the hundred are still alive.
flow.kid: Draw the bottom line and mark five ages. Draw the side line and mark 0 to 100.
flow.context: This step of Three Survival Curves is for drawing the two axes of the graph.

flow.do: 1. Read out the table. Elephant type: 100, 90, 85, 70, 10. Small bird type: 100, 50, 25, 12, 6. Fish type: 100, 3, 2, 1, 1. 2. Your child plots each row in its own colour and joins the dots.
flow.say: These numbers are made up, but each row has the shape that scientists find for that kind of animal. Plot one row at a time.
flow.kid: Plot the elephant numbers and join them. Then the bird numbers. Then the fish numbers.
flow.parent: The fish line drops almost straight down and then runs along the bottom. That is correct. Biologists call the three shapes Type 1, Type 2 and Type 3.
flow.context: This step of Three Survival Curves is for plotting the three rows of numbers and joining the dots.

flow.do: 1. Ask when most deaths happen on each line. 2. Ask which line fits a human in India today, a sparrow and a salmon. 3. Ask which line fits a mother who lays 300 million eggs. 4. Ask which line humans had 200 years ago, when many children died young.
flow.say: On each line, when do most of the hundred die? Which line fits us? Which fits a salmon?
flow.kid: When do most die on each line? Which line fits a human? A sparrow? A salmon?

ask.q: Which line fitted humans 200 years ago, and what changed it?
good: Something between the bird line and the fish line, because many babies and children died.
Clean water, vaccines and medicines moved us to the elephant line.

flow.parent: A survival curve is not fixed for ever. In India around 1900, about one baby in five died before the age of one. Today about 97 in 100 live.

check.q: A survival curve drops almost to zero in the first weeks of life and then runs flat. Which animal does it fit?
check.why: A hilsa lays a million or more eggs with no care, and nearly all the young die in the first weeks. Elephants and humans today mostly survive when young and die late in life, so their curve stays high and drops at the end.

flow.context: This is the last step of Three Survival Curves. Here you match each curve to real animals.

activities.title: The Salt Switch: what does salt water do to living cells?
activities.context: A salmon moves from a river to the salty sea and back. In this activity strips of potato stand for a body made of living cells. You find out what plain water and salt water do to them, and why a fish needs a different body for the river and for the sea.

materials.item: a potato
a knife and a chopping board, for the grown-up
steel or glass tumblers
salt
a teaspoon, a ruler, paper slips and a pencil

activities.record: Make a table with three rows: plain water, sea-strength water and very salty water. For each, write the length of the strip before and after, and how easily it bends. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why.

setup.art: A grown-up cutting a peeled potato into three equal strips, each about 6 centimetres long and as thick as a pencil.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts three potato strips of the same size.

setup.art: Three tumblers of water on paper slips labelled 'plain', 'sea' and 'very salty', with a potato strip in each.
setup.caption: 2. Put one strip in plain water, one in sea-strength water and one in very salty water.

setup.art: A child holding a potato strip by one end, the strip drooping, beside a stiff strip held level.
setup.caption: 3. After 40 minutes, take the strips out and see how each one bends.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up peels the potato and cuts three strips. Each is about 6 centimetres long and as thick as a pencil. 2. Your child measures each strip and bends each one gently. 3. Fill three tumblers three quarters full of water. 4. Leave the first plain. Stir 1 heaped teaspoon of salt into the second. Stir 4 heaped teaspoons into the third. 5. Label them 'plain', 'sea' and 'very salty'.
flow.say: A potato is made of living cells, full of water. Feel how stiff the strips are. One tumbler is about as salty as the sea, and one is much saltier.
flow.kid: Measure each strip. Bend each one gently. Put salt in two tumblers. Label all three.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Salt Switch. Here you cut three potato strips and make three tumblers of water with different amounts of salt.

flow.do: 1. Ask which strip will be stiffest and which softest after 40 minutes, and why. 2. Write the guesses. 3. Put one strip in each tumbler.
flow.say: After forty minutes, which strip will be the stiffest? Which will be the softest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which strip ends up stiffest. Guess which ends up softest. Say why. Put the strips in.
flow.context: This step of the Salt Switch is for guessing. You guess before the strips go into the water.

flow.do: 1. Leave the tumblers for 40 minutes. 2. Do another part of the unit while you wait.
flow.say: Now we wait forty minutes. The cells need time.
flow.kid: Leave the tumblers for 40 minutes.
flow.context: This step of the Salt Switch is a wait of 40 minutes while the potato strips sit in the water.

flow.do: 1. Take out each strip and dry it on a cloth. 2. Hold each strip by one end and see how far it droops. 3. Measure each strip again. 4. Write the results in the table.
flow.say: Hold each one by the end. Which droops most? Which is stiffest? Has any strip changed length?
flow.kid: Take the strips out. Hold each by one end. Which droops most? Measure them again.
flow.parent: The strip from plain water stays stiff or gets a little stiffer. The sea-strength strip bends more. The very salty strip is limp and may be a millimetre or two shorter. If you see no difference, leave them for another 30 minutes.
flow.context: This step of the Salt Switch is for the results. You bend and measure each potato strip after 40 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for the three sentences. 2. Ask where the water in the limp strip went. 3. Only then read the card 'From fresh water to salt water' together.
flow.say: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why. Where did the water from the limp strip go? What does that mean for a fish in the sea?
flow.kid: Say what you guessed, what you saw, and why. Then say what this means for a fish in the sea.

ask.q: Where did the water from the limp strip go?
good: Out of the potato cells and into the salty water.
Water moved towards the saltier side.

check.q: A potato strip goes limp in very salty water. Why?
options: Water moves out of the cells towards the salt
The potato soaks up too much water
check.why: Water moves through the thin skin of each cell towards the saltier side. This is osmosis. The cells lose water and go soft. Choosing 'soaks up too much water' gets the direction the wrong way round: that happens, a little, in plain water.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Salt Switch. Here you explain the results and link them to a fish in the sea.

projects.title: The Dal Jar Watch: a whole life cycle inside one seed (if you find pulse beetles)
projects.context: Pulse beetles are small brown beetles that live in stored whole moong, cowpea and chana. The adults do not need to eat, and they live about ten days. In this five-week project you keep some in a jar, count their eggs and count how many of those eggs become adults.

materials.item: whole moong, cowpea or chana with pulse beetles: a handful with small round holes and at least five live beetles
clean whole seeds of the same kind, with no holes
a glass or clear plastic jar
a small cup or katori
thin cotton cloth and rubber bands, to cover the jar and the cup
a hand lens
a notebook and a pencil

projects.safety: Keep the jar and the cup covered with cloth, and well away from the shelf where food is stored, so that the beetles do not spread to other jars.

schedule.what: Find the beetles. Set up the jar with holed seeds, live beetles and 60 clean seeds.
Take out 20 seeds that have eggs on them. Count the eggs with a hand lens. Keep these 20 seeds in the covered cup.
Look at the 20 seeds again. Look for eggs that have turned white, and for dark patches under the seed skin.
Count the round holes in the 20 seeds, and any adults in the cup.
Count the holes again. Work out the share of eggs that became adults. Empty the jar and the cup outdoors.

projects.record: Keep a page for each visit, with the date, a photo or drawing and your counts. On the last day write two numbers: the eggs you counted on the 20 seeds, and the holes in those same seeds. Then write the share of eggs that became adults.

setup.art: A jar of whole moong on a table with a few small brown beetles walking on the seeds, and some seeds with neat round holes.
setup.caption: 1. Find seeds with round holes and at least five live beetles.

setup.art: The jar covered with thin cotton cloth held by a rubber band, standing on a shelf away from the kitchen.
setup.caption: 2. Add 60 clean seeds. Cover the jar with cloth.

setup.art: A child looking through a hand lens at a green moong seed with two tiny white specks glued on.
setup.caption: 3. After four days, find the eggs: tiny white specks glued to the seeds.

setup.art: Twenty moong seeds in a small cup, several with one neat round hole, and a small brown beetle beside them.
setup.caption: 4. Weeks later, count the round holes the new adults cut to get out.

flow.do: 1. Look in jars of old whole moong, cowpea or chana for seeds with small round holes, or ask at a grocery shop. 2. Put a handful of these seeds and at least five live beetles in the jar. 3. Add 60 clean seeds of the same kind. 4. Cover the jar with cloth and a rubber band. 5. Stand it in a warm, shaded place away from stored food. 6. Your child looks closely at one beetle and one holed seed with the hand lens.
flow.say: These beetles are adults. They will not eat anything now. What do you think made the round holes in the seeds?
flow.kid: Find seeds with round holes and live beetles. Put them in the jar with 60 clean seeds. Cover the jar.
flow.parent: If you find holed seeds and no live beetles, keep the seeds in the covered jar for two weeks. Adults often come out of seeds that look whole. If none come, skip this project.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Dal Jar Watch. Here you find pulse beetles and set up the jar.

flow.do: 1. Tip some seeds onto a plate. 2. With the hand lens, find clean seeds that now have tiny white specks glued on. These are eggs. 3. Pick out 20 seeds with eggs. 4. Count every egg on the 20 seeds and write the total. 5. Put the 20 seeds in the cup and cover it with cloth.
flow.say: Each white speck is one egg, glued to the seed by a mother. Let's count every egg on our twenty seeds.
flow.kid: Find 20 seeds with white specks. The specks are eggs. Count all the eggs. Write the number.

ask.q: How many adults do you think will come out of these eggs, and why?
good: Fewer than the eggs, because some will not hatch.
Maybe only one from each seed, because a seed is small.

flow.parent: A female lays up to about a hundred eggs. Each egg is about half a millimetre long. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is day 5 of the Dal Jar Watch. Here you find the eggs, count them on 20 seeds and set those seeds apart.

flow.do: 1. Look at the 20 seeds with the hand lens. 2. Look for eggs that have turned from clear to solid white. 3. Hold a seed up to the light and look for a dark patch under the skin. 4. Take a photo of what you see, or tell your grown-up what you see.
flow.say: The young beetle never walks on the outside. So where do you think the young one went when the egg hatched?
flow.kid: Look at the 20 seeds. Which eggs have turned white? Where did the young one go?
flow.parent: The young beetle, called a larva, bites straight down through the bottom of the egg into the seed. The larva eats and grows inside the seed. An egg turns white when the larva has hatched and gone in.
flow.context: This is day 15 of the Dal Jar Watch. Here you look for signs of the young beetles inside the seeds.

flow.do: 1. Count the round holes in the 20 seeds. 2. Count any adult beetles in the cup. 3. Write both numbers.
flow.say: Each round hole is a door that one new adult cut to get out. How many doors so far? Is that more or fewer than you guessed?
flow.kid: Count the round holes in the 20 seeds. Count the adults in the cup. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: In warm weather the first adults come out about four weeks after the eggs were laid. In cool weather it can take seven weeks. If there are no holes yet, check again each week.
flow.context: This is day 29 of the Dal Jar Watch. Here you count the first new adults and the holes they came out of.

flow.do: 1. Count the holes in the 20 seeds one last time. 2. Write the share: holes out of eggs. 3. Ask why some eggs did not become adults. 4. Take the jar and the cup outdoors. Empty them onto soil well away from the house.
flow.say: Let's find out how many of the eggs became adults.
flow.kid: Count the holes. Say how many eggs became adults.

ask.q: Why did some eggs not become adults?
good: Some eggs did not hatch.
When several larvae share one small seed, there is not enough food for all.

ask.q: Why does the adult not need to eat?
good: The larva stored enough food in the body while inside the seed.
The adult only has to mate and lay eggs, and that takes a few days.

check.q: A pulse beetle adult lives about ten days and eats nothing. Which stage did the eating?
options: The adult, before we saw her
check.why: The larva eats the inside of the seed for about three weeks and stores food in the body. The adult lives on that store. A mayfly and a periodical cicada divide their lives in a similar way: a long feeding stage and a short breeding stage.

flow.context: This is the last day of the Dal Jar Watch. Here you work out what share of the eggs became adults.

challenges.title: The Fish Pass: get a hilsa past a barrage
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. Hilsa swim up rivers from the sea to spawn. A barrage is a low dam across a river, and a fish cannot swim up its wall of falling water. Here you build a stair of small pools that would let a fish climb round the barrage.
challenges.problem: A barrage 12 centimetres high blocks your river. Build a path of pools from the top to the bottom. Water poured into the top pool must flow through every pool in turn. No drop between pools may be higher than 3 centimetres, because hilsa do not leap as salmon do.
constraints: The top pool stands 12 centimetres above the bottom.
No drop from one pool to the next is more than 3 centimetres.
Every pool must hold water at least 1 centimetre deep, so that a fish could rest there.
The water must run from pool to pool, not spill onto the floor.
materials: books or boxes, to make the heights
steel katoris, jar lids or small plates, for pools
kitchen foil or pieces of cardboard, for spouts and channels
a jug of water and a tumbler
a large tray, or do it on the bathroom floor
general: Make a stair of four or five katoris on piles of books, each one 3 centimetres lower than the last.
Tilt each katori a little towards the next, so that the water leaves from one side.
Fold a small foil spout on the rim of each pool, to guide the water into the next.
creative: Build one long, gentle channel that winds round the barrage like a side stream, lined with a wet towel. Real 'nature-like' fish passes work this way.
Build a zigzag, so that the stair fits into a small space.
Build a fish lift: a pool that is filled at the bottom, carried up by hand and emptied at the top. Some real dams have fish lifts.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own fish pass. Plan it first by laying out the pools and saying each drop's height, or draw it and label every drop. Build it, pour one tumbler of water in at the top and watch. Where does the water run too fast for a fish? How would you slow it?

setup.art: A pile of books 12 centimetres high with a ruler beside it and a katori on top, on a large tray.
setup.caption: 1. Build the barrage: a top pool 12 centimetres above the tray.

setup.art: A stair of five katoris on lower and lower piles of books, each tilted a little, with small foil spouts.
setup.caption: 2. Build pools down to the tray. No drop may be more than 3 centimetres.

setup.art: A child pouring water from a tumbler into the top katori, with water running from pool to pool down the stair.
setup.caption: 3. Pour water in at the top and see whether it runs through every pool.

flow.do: 1. Put a pile of books 12 centimetres high on the tray, with a katori on top. 2. Pour water into the katori until it overflows. 3. Watch where the water goes. 4. Ask whether a fish could swim up that fall, and what a fish would need.
flow.say: This is the barrage. Watch the water fall. Could a fish that cannot jump get up there? What would she need?
flow.kid: Build the barrage. Pour water over the top. Could a fish swim up? What would she need?
flow.parent: Do this on a large tray or on the bathroom floor. Use old books or boxes, and put a plastic sheet over them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Fish Pass. Here you build a model barrage and see why a fish cannot climb it.

flow.do: 1. Look at the usual ideas: a stair of katoris, tilted, with foil spouts. 2. Your child chooses one and says why it should work. 3. Build it. 4. Measure every drop with the ruler. 5. Pour one tumbler of water slowly into the top pool.
flow.say: Which idea will you try first? Why should it work? Measure each drop. Then pour, and watch where the water goes.
flow.kid: Pick an idea. Say why it should work. Build it. Measure each drop. Pour the water.

ask.q: Why does a real fish pass have pools, and not just one long slope?
good: A fish can rest in each pool before the next climb.
The water slows down in each pool, so the fish is not swept back.

flow.context: This step of the Fish Pass tests one of the usual designs, a stair of small pools.

flow.do: 1. Your child plans a pass of their own by laying out the pools, or by drawing it. 2. They build it and test it with one tumbler of water. 3. They check the rule with the ruler: no drop is more than 3 centimetres, and the water runs through every pool. 4. They change one thing and test again.
flow.say: Now design your own. Plan it first. After the test, change one thing to make it better, and say why you chose that thing.
flow.kid: Design your own fish pass. Plan it, build it and test it. Change one thing and test again.
flow.parent: The hard part is making the water leave each pool at one place. A small foil spout or a tilt solves it. Real hilsa are harder to help than this model suggests, and engineers are still testing designs for them.

check.q: Why does a dam or barrage with no fish pass harm fish like hilsa and salmon?
options: It makes the water too clean
They cannot reach the places upstream where they spawn
It makes the river too deep
check.why: These fish must swim upstream to lay their eggs in the right kind of river bed. A wall across the river stops them, so fewer young are produced. A fish pass gives them a way round.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Fish Pass. Here you build, test and improve your own design.

challenges.title: Design a Life Cycle: fit a timetable to a home
challenges.context: This is a design challenge on paper. Every life cycle in this unit fits the dangers and the food of one kind of home. Here you are given a home, and you design a life cycle that would work there.
challenges.problem: Choose one home. Design an animal's timetable for it. Decide how many eggs, how big, how much care, how long the young stage lasts, when to breed and whether to breed once or many times. Give a reason for every choice.
constraints: Home 1: a rain pool that holds water for four months and is dry mud for eight months, every year.
Home 2: a forest full of hungry birds, where the only food for your young is thin sap in tree roots.
Home 3: the deep, cold sea floor, with very little food and very few predators.
Your animal has a fixed egg budget. She can have many small eggs or a few big ones, and not many big ones.
materials: your Life Bars drawing, if you have done it
general: For the pool: grow up fast and breed before the water goes.
For the forest: come out in a big crowd, so that the birds cannot eat everyone.
For the deep sea: lay a few large eggs and guard them.
creative: For the pool: lay eggs that can wait in dry mud for months. Annual killifish do this.
For the forest: stay underground for many years, so that the birds cannot grow in number on you. Periodical cicadas do this.
For the deep sea: guard the eggs for a very long time. One deep-sea octopus was watched guarding her eggs for 53 months.
challenges.your_turn: Now show your animal's life as a bar, like the Life Bars. Use a paper strip or a drawing. Mark each stage and how long it lasts. Then swap homes: put your animal in one of the other two homes. What goes wrong first?

setup.art: Three small pictures side by side: a muddy rain pool with cracked edges, a forest floor with birds in the trees, and a dark sea floor with a few rocks.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one of the three homes.

setup.art: A child's drawing of an invented animal with a life bar underneath, split into stages and labelled with times.
setup.caption: 2. Design the timetable and show it as a life bar, with a reason for every choice.

flow.do: 1. Read out the three homes. 2. Your child chooses one. 3. Ask what the biggest danger is in that home, and what the food is like.
flow.say: Which home will you design for? What is the biggest danger there? What is the food like? Those two answers will shape everything.
flow.kid: Choose a home. What is the biggest danger there? What is the food like?
flow.context: This is the first step of Design a Life Cycle. Here you choose a home and name its dangers and its food.

flow.do: 1. Your child decides each part of the timetable and writes a reason beside it. 2. They tell you what the animal looks like. 3. They show the life as a bar on paper, with each stage marked.
flow.say: How many eggs, and how big? Will you guard them? How long is the young stage? Will you breed once or many times? Give me a reason for each.
flow.kid: Decide the eggs, the care, the young stage and the breeding. Say a reason for each. Show the life as a bar.

ask.q: Why did you choose to breed once, or many times?
good: Once, because the adult cannot live through the dry months anyway.
Many times, because the deep sea is safe and an adult can live long.

flow.context: This step of Design a Life Cycle is for designing the timetable and drawing it as a life bar.

flow.do: 1. Read the usual and the creative solutions for the chosen home. 2. Compare them with your child's design. 3. Ask what would go wrong if the animal moved to one of the other homes.
flow.say: Here is how some real animals solve it. What is the same as yours? Now move your animal to another home. What goes wrong first?
flow.kid: Compare your design with a real animal's. Now move your animal to another home. What goes wrong?
flow.parent: There is no single right design. A good answer gives a reason from the home for each choice. The swap shows that a timetable is good only for the home it fits.

check.q: A fish lives in a pool that is dry for eight months of every year. Which timetable fits best?
options: Grow slowly and breed at ten years old
Grow fast, and lay eggs that can wait in dry mud
Lay one large egg and guard it all year
check.why: The adults cannot survive the dry months, so they must breed within one wet season. Eggs that can wait in dry mud carry the animal through to the next rain. Slow growth or a year of guarding needs water all year.

flow.context: This is the last step of Design a Life Cycle. Here you compare your design with real animals and test it in another home.

worksheets.title: Strange life cycles: cicada, salmon and jellyfish (core)

items.p: What is unusual about the life cycle of a periodical cicada?
opts: The whole population comes out in one year
The eggs are laid deep underground
items.why: All the nymphs of a brood grow up together and come out in the same few evenings. The adults live only about a month, and the eggs are laid in twigs. Choosing '17 years as adults' mixes up the nymph and the adult.

items.p: True or false: a cicada nymph sleeps through her years underground.
items.why: False. The nymph digs, drinks sap from roots, grows and sheds her skin four times. She even counts the years by changes in the tree's sap.

items.p: When so many prey arrive that predators eat until they are full, it is called predator ____.
a: satiation
items.why: Satiation means being full. Most of the prey are left alive because the predators can eat only so many.

items.p: Put the stages of a Pacific salmon's life in order.
items: Egg in the gravel of a stream
Adult back in the home stream, spawning
Silver smolt swimming to the sea
Young fish in the river or a lake
a: Egg in the gravel of a stream
Young fish in the river or a lake
Silver smolt swimming to the sea
Adult growing in the ocean
Adult back in the home stream, spawning
items.why: A salmon hatches in fresh water, grows in the sea and returns to fresh water to spawn. A strong answer can say what changes in the body at the smolt stage.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: Spawn
to release eggs or sperm into water
Smolt
a young salmon ready for salt water
Polyp
the fixed, young stage of a jellyfish
Medusa
the swimming, adult stage of a jellyfish
Brood
all the cicadas that come out in one year in one region
items.why: These words are used all through the unit. A strong answer could give an animal for each.

items.p: Sort these animals: breeds once in a life, or breeds many times.
items.why: Pacific salmon, mayflies and octopuses put everything into one breeding and die. Hens, elephants and crows breed again and again.

items.p: How does a salmon find the stream where she hatched?
opts: By remembering what it looks like
items.why: She learned the smell of her stream as a young fish and follows it back. Her parents died years before, so nobody leads her.

items.p: A bird eats the same number from a crowd of 10 and of 80. What does this mean for each cicada?
items.a: Each cicada in the crowd of 80 is much safer. The same small meal is shared among eight times as many, so each one's chance of being eaten is about eight times smaller.
items.why: A strong answer talks about the share eaten, or each one's chance, and not only the number eaten.

items.p: A bird eats 8 rajma from a crowd of 80. How many are left?
items.why: 80 − 8 = 72. That is 72 out of 80 left, or 9 out of every 10.

items.p: Draw the life cycle of the immortal jellyfish. Add the one arrow that makes it unusual.
items.art: An empty circle with five blank boxes round it for the stages of a jellyfish's life.
items.a: A circle of stages: egg, swimming larva, polyp, young medusa, adult medusa. One extra arrow runs back from the adult medusa to the polyp.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the usual cycle first and then the backward arrow from medusa to polyp. An arrow from medusa to egg is the usual way, by breeding, and is not the unusual one.

items.p: Three of these give their young no care. Which one cares for her young?
items.why: An elephant feeds her calf with milk for two years or more and the herd guards the calf. The sunfish, the hilsa and the turtle leave their eggs.

items.p: True or false: a fish who lays a million eggs usually leaves about a million grown-up young.
items.why: False. Nearly all the eggs and young are eaten or starve. Where the number of fish stays steady, about two from each pair grow up to breed.

items.p: The immortal jellyfish can turn from adult back to young. Why is 'immortal' still not quite right?
opts: She can still be eaten or fall ill
She lives for only one year
Nobody has ever seen the change
items.why: She can escape death from old age, but fish and sea slugs eat her, and disease kills her. The change has been seen many times in laboratories.

items.p: On a drawing of a salmon's journey, label where she hatches, where she grows and where she spawns.
items.art: A simple map of a stream running down from mountains to a river and out to the sea, with three blank label lines.
a: Hatches: in the gravel of a stream
Grows: in the ocean
Spawns: in the same stream where she hatched
items.why: A strong answer puts hatching and spawning at the same place. That return to the home stream is the unusual part.

items.p: Three people talk about which stage is the real cicada.

views.says: The real cicada is the winged one who sings. The nymph is only on the way to becoming her.
The real cicada is the nymph. She is a nymph for nearly all of her life.
Both are the same animal with the same genes. 'Real' is our word, and the cicada has no use for it.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Use your Life Bars drawing as evidence. Then say what one of the others has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the Life Bars drawing: the nymph stage is nearly all of the life, and the winged stage is the last month. It chooses one view, gives that evidence, and says what another view has right.
items.why: All three have a point. The winged stage is the one that breeds, the nymph is the stage that lasts, and both are one animal with the same genes.

worksheets.title: Strange life cycles: evidence and reasons (stretch)

items.p: The crowd protects cicadas. How does the 17-year wait help as well?
opts: Predators cannot multiply on such rare food
Nymphs need 17 years to learn to fly
Trees make sap only every 17 years
Birds forget what cicadas taste like
items.why: If cicadas came every year, more of the predators' young would be fed, and predator numbers would rise. A meal that comes once in 17 years cannot support extra predators in between.

items.p: Scientists made peach trees flower twice in one year. Cicadas on their roots came out a year early. What does this show?
items.a: It shows that the nymphs count the trees' yearly cycles and not real time. Two flowerings in one year counted as two years.
items.why: A strong answer says what the cicadas were counting, and why two flowerings fooled them.

items.p: Salmon with plugged noses chose between two streams at random. What does this show?
opts: They need smell to find home
items.why: Fish with open noses chose their own branch, and fish who could not smell could not. So smell is what they use. Choosing 'cotton makes fish ill' is a fair worry, and it is why the open-nosed fish were handled the same way.

items.p: Water moves through the thin skin of a cell towards the ____ side.
a: saltier
more salty
salty
items.why: Water moves towards the side with more salt. This movement is called osmosis.

items.p: True or false: in the sea, a fish keeps losing water from her body to the salty water around her.
items.why: True. The sea is about three times as salty as her blood, so water moves out. She drinks sea water and pumps the extra salt out at her gills.

items.p: Sort these animals by the shape of their survival curve.
items.why: Animals with many eggs and no care lose most young in the first weeks. Animals with few, cared-for young mostly live until they are old.

items.p: A 13-year brood and a 17-year brood came out together in 2024. In which year will they next come out together?
items.why: They meet again after 13 × 17 = 221 years, because 13 and 17 share no factor. 2024 + 221 = 2245.

items.p: Match each animal to the strange part of their timetable.
pairs: Axolotl
breeds while the body still looks young
Aphid
daughters are born with no father
Clownfish
a male can become a female
Annual killifish
eggs wait for months in dry mud
Tsetse fly
one baby at a time, fed on a milk-like liquid
items.why: Each of these animals changes a different part of the usual timetable: when to grow up, whether a father is needed, which sex to be, how to wait, or how many young to have.

items.p: A salmon dies in a mountain stream. Explain how part of her body can end up inside a tree.
items.a: Bears and birds carry dead salmon into the forest and leave parts of them. Insects, fungi and bacteria break the body down. The nitrogen from her body goes into the soil, and tree roots take it up.
items.why: A strong answer gives the steps in order. An excellent one adds how we know: trees near salmon streams hold the heavier kind of nitrogen that comes from the sea.

items.p: Which of these animals is semelparous?
items.why: A mayfly breeds once and dies within a day or two. A hen, a hilsa and a crow can all breed again. Choosing the hilsa mixes her up with the Pacific salmon.

items.p: Draw three survival curves on one graph: elephant type, small bird type and fish type. Label each line.
items.art: Two empty graph axes: age along the bottom and 'number still alive' up the side.
items.a: The elephant line stays high and falls near the end. The bird line slopes down steadily. The fish line drops almost to zero at once and then runs flat.
items.why: A strong drawing starts all three lines at the same point, at 100, and gives each a clearly different shape.

items.p: Put the steps of the immortal jellyfish's backward change in order.
items: The ball grows into a polyp
Her bell shrinks into a small ball
The polyp buds off new medusae
The medusa is starved, hurt or old
The ball sinks and sticks to the bottom
a: The medusa is starved, hurt or old
Her bell shrinks into a small ball
The ball sinks and sticks to the bottom
The ball grows into a polyp
The polyp buds off new medusae
items.why: The old body is the material for the new polyp, so the shrinking and settling come before the polyp grows.

items.p: Three of these animals appear in a huge crowd at the same time. Which one does not?
items.why: Winged termites, periodical cicadas and nesting olive ridley turtles all arrive together in great numbers. A tiger lives and hunts alone.

items.p: A muscle cell and a nerve cell in the same body differ mainly in what?
items.why: Nearly every cell in a body carries the same genes. The kind of cell depends on which genes are in use. Choosing 'which genes they carry' is the old idea that John Gurdon's frog experiment showed to be wrong.

items.p: Three people talk about catching hilsa as the fish swim upriver to spawn.

views.says: This is the season when the fish come to us, and they sell for the best price. My family lives on this catch.
A fish caught before she spawns leaves no young. Stop fishing for the few weeks of spawning, and there will be more fish every year.

views.who: A woman who sells fish at the market
views.says: A ban is fair only if fishing families are given food or other work for those weeks.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Use what you know about spawning as evidence. Then say what one of the others has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the life cycle: a fish caught on the way upriver has not yet laid her eggs, so that year's young are lost too. It also takes seriously the fishing family's need to eat during a ban.
items.why: The scientist is right about the fish, and the other two are right about the people. Several states and Bangladesh now stop hilsa fishing for some weeks of the spawning season, and argue about how to support fishing families then.

worksheets.title: Strange life cycles: argued ideas and big numbers (challenge)

items.p: No periodical cicada has a 12-year cycle. Give two different ideas scientists have about why 13 and 17 work better.
items.a: One idea: a predator with a cycle of 2, 3, 4 or 6 years would meet a 12-year cicada every time, but rarely a 13-year one. Another idea: broods with prime cycles rarely come out in the same year, so they seldom mix and spoil each other's timing.
items.why: A strong answer gives two ideas and says that scientists have not settled which is right. A third idea, that 13 and 17 are partly chance, is also a good answer.

items.p: The bird in the Crowd Test was limited only by time. What else limits a real bird?
items.why: A real bird stops eating when she is full. That limit, like the time limit in the model, means a predator can eat only so many.

items.p: A pair of frogs lays 1,000 eggs. If every egg grew up, how many pairs would the next generation have?
items.why: 1,000 frogs make 1,000 ÷ 2 = 500 pairs. If each pair again laid 1,000 eggs, there would be 500,000 frogs in the generation after.

items.p: A pair of frogs lays 1,000 eggs every year. Yet the pond has about the same number of frogs each year. Explain.
items.a: Nearly all the eggs and tadpoles die. Fish, insects and birds eat them, and some starve. On average only about two from each pair's eggs live to breed, which just replaces the parents.
items.why: A strong answer gives the number that must survive, about two per pair, and says what happens to the rest.

items.p: True or false: a gut cell still carries the instructions for building a whole animal.
items.why: True. John Gurdon put the nucleus of a tadpole's gut cell into an egg, and a whole frog grew. Nearly every cell keeps the full set of genes and uses only some of them.

items.p: Landlocked sockeye salmon never go to sea, yet they die after spawning. What does this suggest?
opts: The long journey alone is not the cause
items.why: These fish make only a short trip and still die. So the death is set off from inside the body, by hormones, when the fish spawns. The journey makes it harder but does not cause it.

items.p: Sort these statements: settled by evidence, or still argued about.
items: Cicada nymphs count the trees' yearly cycles
Prime cycles protect cicadas from predators with cycles
Salmon follow smell to their home stream
Salmon steer by the Earth's magnetism in the open ocean
Some animals do not age at all
A medusa of the immortal jellyfish can become a polyp
items.why: A settled statement has been tested many times with the same result. An argued one has some evidence, and scientists still disagree about it.

items.p: Draw a fish in a river and the same fish in the sea. Add arrows for where water moves.
items.art: Two outlines of the same fish, one labelled 'river' and one labelled 'sea', with nothing else drawn.
items.a: In the river, the arrows point into the fish, and she passes a lot of watery urine. In the sea, the arrows point out of the fish, and she drinks sea water and pumps salt out at the gills.
items.why: A strong drawing has the arrows pointing towards the saltier side each time: into the fish in the river, and out of the fish in the sea.

items.p: Growth by multiplying again and again is called ____ growth.
a: exponential
items.why: Exponential growth starts slowly and then becomes enormous. It is why most young of every kind of animal must die before they breed.

items.p: Put these mothers in order, from the fewest eggs or young at one time to the most.
a: Asian elephant
Olive ridley turtle
Sockeye salmon
Hilsa
Ocean sunfish
items.why: An elephant has 1 calf. An olive ridley lays about 100 eggs, a sockeye about 3,000, a hilsa about a million and an ocean sunfish up to about 300 million.

items.p: A polyp grows from an old medusa. Is she the same animal or a new one? Give one reason for each side.
items.a: The same animal: the polyp is made from the medusa's own cells and has the same genes, and no egg or parent is involved. A new animal: the body has a different shape and way of life, and the polyp buds off many medusae, so one has become many.
items.why: There is no agreed answer. A strong answer gives a real reason on each side and says which the writer finds stronger.

items.p: A girl picks the home katori correctly 3 times out of 3. Why is that good evidence?
opts: Three lucky guesses in a row are unlikely
The katoris all looked the same
items.why: With three katoris, one guess is right 1 time in 3. Three right guesses in a row happen by luck only about 1 time in 27. So the nose very probably found the smell.

items.p: Match each cause to its effect.
pairs: A tree is made to flower twice in a year
cicadas on its roots come out a year early
A salmon's nose is plugged
she can no longer find her home stream
A medusa is starved
she turns back into a polyp
A potato strip sits in salty water
its cells lose water and go soft
A barrage is built with no fish pass
fish cannot reach their spawning places
items.why: Each pair is a test or a change, and what followed from it. A strong answer can say what each pair tells us.

items.p: On a fish-type survival curve, label where most deaths happen, and where the few breeders are.
items.art: A graph line that drops steeply from 100 at the start to near zero, then runs flat to the right, with two blank label lines.
a: Most deaths: the steep drop at the very start
The breeders: the flat, low part of the line towards the right
items.why: Nearly all the deaths come in the first days and weeks. The few who reach the flat part of the line are the ones who breed.

items.p: Three people talk about whether humans should become young again, as the immortal jellyfish does, if science made it possible.

views.says: If we could reset worn-out cells, nobody would suffer the illnesses of old age. That would be a great good.
If nobody died, our numbers would multiply until there was no room or food. There would be no place for children.
Nobody knows whether the new polyp keeps anything the old medusa learned. If I lost every memory, would the young one be me?

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Use one idea from the science as evidence. Then say what one of the others has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the science: cells can be reset, numbers multiply without limit if nobody dies, and nobody knows what a reset body keeps. It chooses a view and gives a fair point from another.
items.why: This question has no agreed answer. Each view rests on something true from the unit: resetting cells, exponential growth, and what makes an animal the same animal.

quiz.p: Where does a periodical cicada spend most of her life?
opts: In the treetops, as an adult
quiz.why: She is a nymph underground for 13 or 17 years and a winged adult for about a month.

quiz.p: Millions of cicadas come out within a few evenings. How does this help each one?
opts: Predators get full, and most cicadas are left
Their noise frightens every bird away
quiz.why: This is predator satiation. Birds and other predators eat all they can, and that is a small share of a huge crowd. The loud song is for finding mates.

quiz.p: A bird eats 10 insects from a crowd of 20 and 10 from 200. Which crowd is safer to be in?
quiz.why: In the crowd of 20, half are eaten. In the crowd of 200, only 1 in 20 is eaten. The same meal is a much smaller share of the bigger crowd.

quiz.p: What does a young salmon learn before leaving for the sea?
opts: The smell of the home stream
The number of bends in the river
quiz.why: A young salmon imprints on the smell of the home stream and follows it back years later. Her parents died soon after spawning.

quiz.p: Which test best shows whether salmon need smell to find home?
opts: Plug some noses and compare with open noses
Follow one fish up the river
Count the fish in the river
quiz.why: A fair test changes one thing, the sense of smell, and compares two groups. Following one fish or counting fish cannot show which sense is used.

opts: Lives in both river and sea
quiz.why: A semelparous animal, such as a Pacific salmon or a mayfly, puts everything into one breeding. An animal who breeds many times is iteroparous.

quiz.p: Why can it work for a Pacific salmon to spend her whole body on one spawning?
opts: Few would survive a second journey
Eggs cannot hatch unless the parents die
The river is too warm to leave
quiz.why: The return to the sea and a second climb up the river would kill most fish. So a salmon who holds something back for next time usually wastes what she held back.

quiz.p: A mother has a fixed amount of material for eggs. What must she give up to lay more eggs?
quiz.why: The same material can be cut into a few big eggs or many small ones. More eggs means smaller eggs, each with less food for the baby.

quiz.p: Where the number of animals stays steady, about how many young from each pair live to breed?
quiz.why: About two, which just replaces the parents. This is true for an elephant with a few calves and for a fish with a million eggs.

quiz.p: What happens to the cells when the immortal jellyfish turns from a medusa into a polyp?
opts: Many change from one kind of cell into another
All die, and a new egg grows
They stay exactly as they were
They are shed into the sea
quiz.why: The medusa's own cells are reused, and many change kind by switching different genes on. This is called transdifferentiation.

quiz.p: A model uses rajma for cicadas and a child for a bird. What is the best thing to say about its results?
opts: They show an idea that real animals must confirm
They prove what real birds do
They are true only for rajma
quiz.why: A model shows clearly how one idea works. Counts of real cicadas and real birds are still needed, and scientists have made those counts.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still argue about?
opts: Why cicada cycles are 13 and 17 years
Whether salmon return to their home streams
Whether jellyfish have a polyp stage
quiz.why: The other three are well tested. For the prime-numbered cycles there are at least three ideas and no agreement.

Rules on the smallest fish that may be caught let each fish breed at least once before she can be taken.

Doctors can now turn a person's skin or blood cells back into cells that can become any kind. In 2014, the eye doctor Masayo Takahashi in Japan was the first to treat a patient with tissue grown from such cells.
Knowing a pest's timetable tells us when to act. Drying whole dal in hot sun kills the eggs and larvae of pulse beetles before the adults come out.

Fruit growers in the eastern United States know the cicada years in advance. They cover young trees with nets in those years, because egg-laying damages thin twigs.

open_questions.q: Where in a cicada nymph's body is the count of years kept, and how does it reach exactly seventeen?
open_questions.why_open: We know the nymphs count the trees' yearly cycles. Nobody has found the part of the body or the chemicals that store the count.

open_questions.q: Why are periodical cicada cycles 13 and 17 years long?
open_questions.why_open: There are at least three ideas: hiding from predators with cycles, keeping broods apart, and chance. No test has yet ruled any of them out.

open_questions.q: How does a salmon steer across thousands of kilometres of open ocean to her own river mouth?
open_questions.why_open: Smell works only near the river. There is some evidence that salmon sense the Earth's magnetism, but nobody has found the sense organ.

open_questions.q: Does the immortal jellyfish turn back into a polyp in the sea, and how often?
open_questions.why_open: The change has been seen only in laboratories. The medusa is 4 millimetres wide, and nobody has been able to follow one in the wild.

open_questions.q: Could the cells of a mammal be reset safely inside a living body, as the jellyfish's cells are?
open_questions.why_open: In mice, switching on the resetting genes for a short time has made some old tissues work better. Left on too long, the same genes cause tumours.

open_questions.q: Does a polyp keep anything that the medusa learned before the change?
open_questions.why_open: Jellyfish can learn simple things. Nobody has tested whether anything learned survives when the nerve cells are rebuilt.

maths.problem: A periodical cicada is a nymph for 17 years and an adult for 4 weeks. What fraction of her life is adult life? Take a year as 52 weeks.
maths.explain: 17 years is 17 × 52 = 884 weeks. The whole life is 884 + 4 = 888 weeks. The adult part is 4 out of 888. Divide both by 4: that is 1 out of 222.
maths.context: This is about Life Bars, where you drew each animal's life as a bar and shaded the part spent as a youngster.
maths.why_maths: A fraction lets us compare lives of very different lengths. It shows how small a share of the cicada's life the winged stage is.

maths.problem: A bird eats 8 cicadas each evening, whatever the size of the crowd. Sixty cicadas can come out 10 each evening for six evenings, or all on one evening. How many are left alive each way?
maths.answer: 12 are left if they come out ten at a time. 52 are left if they all come out together.
maths.explain: Ten at a time: each evening 10 − 8 = 2 are left, and 6 × 2 = 12. All together: the bird eats 8 on that one evening, and 60 − 8 = 52 are left. On the other five evenings there is nothing to eat.
maths.context: This is about the Crowd Test, where a bird picks rajma 'cicadas' off a towel for ten seconds.
maths.why_maths: Working out both plans with the same rule shows exactly where the difference comes from: the bird's meal is taken six times or once.

maths.problem: In the Crowd Test a bird ate 8 rajma out of 10, and later 10 out of 80. What percentage was eaten each time?
maths.answer: 80 percent of the small crowd, and 12.5 percent of the big crowd.
maths.explain: 8 out of 10 is 80 out of 100, which is 80 percent. 10 out of 80 is 1 out of 8. One eighth of 100 is 12.5, so that is 12.5 percent.
maths.context: This is about the Crowd Test, where a bird picks rajma 'cicadas' off a towel for ten seconds.

chart.title: Made-up example: share of the crowd eaten

maths.why_maths: The numbers eaten, 8 and 10, look alike. Percentages show the real difference in danger for each cicada.

maths.problem: Imagine a 12-year brood and a 16-year brood that both come out this year. After how many years will they next come out together? Compare with a 13-year and a 17-year brood.
maths.answer: After 48 years for 12 and 16. After 221 years for 13 and 17.
maths.explain: List the multiples of 16: 16, 32, 48. The first one that 12 also divides is 48. For 13 and 17, no number divides both, so the first shared multiple is 13 × 17 = 221. Broods with prime cycles meet far less often.
maths.context: This is about the game Emerge!, where broods of cicadas choose a year from 12 to 18 to come out.
maths.why_maths: Common multiples tell us how often two cycles fall in the same year. This is the heart of two of the ideas about prime-numbered cycles.

maths.problem: In the Home Stream Test, each cup is 10 times weaker than the one before. The first cup is 1 part in 10. Which cup in the row would be 1 part in 10 billion?
maths.explain: Each cup adds one zero: 10, 100, 1,000 and so on. Ten billion is 10,000,000,000, which has ten zeros. So it is the tenth cup. Salmon have followed a smell about that weak.
maths.context: This is about the Home Stream Test, where you mix a smell with more and more water until your nose loses it.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying by ten again and again reaches huge numbers in a few steps. It lets us compare our nose with a salmon's.

maths.problem: In the Home Stream Test there are three katoris, and one holds the smell. If you only guess, what is the chance of picking the right one three times in a row?
maths.explain: One guess is right 1 time in 3. For two in a row, multiply: 1/3 × 1/3 = 1/9. For three in a row: 1/9 × 1/3 = 1/27. So three right picks are very unlikely to be luck.
maths.context: This is about the Home Stream Test, where you pick the katori with the smell from two katoris of plain water.
maths.why_maths: Knowing the chance of a lucky result tells us how far to trust the test.

maths.problem: A pair of frogs lays 1,000 eggs. Suppose every egg grows up, pairs off and lays 1,000 eggs too. How many frogs hatch in the third generation?
maths.explain: First generation: 1,000 frogs, which is 500 pairs. Second generation: 500 × 1,000 = 500,000 frogs, which is 250,000 pairs. Third generation: 250,000 × 1,000 = 250,000,000 frogs.
maths.context: This is about the card 'If every egg lived'. It asks what would happen if no young animals died.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying again and again shows why nearly all young must die: no pond or country could hold the numbers.

warmup.q: Name an animal that breeds once and dies.
warmup.a: A Pacific salmon, a mayfly, an octopus or a periodical cicada.

warmup.q: What can the medusa of the immortal jellyfish do?
warmup.a: Turn back into a polyp, the young stage.

warmup.q: Which way does water move through a cell's skin?
warmup.a: Towards the saltier side. This is osmosis.

quiz: A periodical cicada sleeps for 17 years.
The nymph is awake: digging, feeding, growing and counting the years.
13 and 17 are prime numbers.
Each can be divided exactly only by 1 and by itself.
A Pacific salmon spawns many times.
She spawns once and dies within days or weeks.
A salmon finds her home stream mainly by smell.
Fish with plugged noses could not choose the right stream.
A hilsa swims up rivers from the sea to spawn.
Hilsa swim up the Godavari, the Hooghly and the Padma in the monsoon.
A fish that lays a million eggs leaves a million adults.
Nearly all are eaten. About two per pair live to breed.
A mother can lay many eggs that are also big.
Her material for eggs is limited, so more eggs means smaller eggs.
The immortal jellyfish cannot be killed.
She can be eaten or fall ill. She can only escape death from old age.
A skin cell and a nerve cell carry the same genes.
They differ in which genes are switched on.
Adult mayflies have no working mouths.
They live a day or two, and only mate and lay eggs.
odd: The salmon, the mayfly and the octopus breed once and die, but a hen breeds many times.
13, 17 and 19 are prime numbers, but 2, 3, 4 and 6 all divide 12.
Egg, smolt and spawner are stages of a salmon, but a polyp is a stage of a jellyfish.
The first three arrive in huge crowds at the same time, but a tiger lives alone.
The sunfish, the hilsa and the frog lay many eggs and give no care, but an elephant has one calf and cares for years.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that a life cycle can run backwards? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: For as long as people had studied animals, they took one thing for granted. A life cycle runs one way. The young become adults, and an adult never becomes young again. In the 1980s two students in Italy, Christian Sommer and Giorgio Bavestrello, were keeping tiny jellyfish called Turritopsis in jars of sea water. The adults, called medusae, should have bred and died. Instead, the students found polyps on the bottom of the jars. Polyps are the young, fixed stage. They watched closely. A medusa that was starved or hurt shrank into a ball, sank, stuck to the glass and grew into a polyp. They reported it in 1992. In 1996, Stefano Piraino, Ferdinando Boero and their team showed that medusae of every age could do this. They also showed that the cells change from one kind into another. Later Shin Kubota in Japan kept one colony going back and forth ten times in two years.
how_we_found_out.who: Christian Sommer and Giorgio Bavestrello, who first saw it. Stefano Piraino, Ferdinando Boero, Brigitte Aeschbach and Volker Schmid, who showed how the cells change. Shin Kubota, who kept a colony changing back again and again.
how_we_found_out.when: The 1980s (first seen), 1992 (first report), 1996 (the study of the cells) and 2011 (Kubota's report of ten changes)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That an adult animal can never go back to being young, because growing up runs only one way. Medusae in jars turned back into polyps in front of the scientists.
how_we_found_out.art: Two students bending over a glass jar of sea water in a small laboratory, with tiny polyps on the bottom of the jar where they expected only swimming jellyfish.

roots.context: We have been learning about animals whose lives are timed very differently from ours. Now we ask what these timetables tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In Life Bars, almost the whole of the cicada's bar was the nymph, and the winged adult was the last millimetre. The mayfly's adult was one pencil line. For these animals the young stage is nearly the whole life, and the adult is a short last stage for breeding. So a nymph is not an unfinished cicada. The nymph is the cicada, for nearly all of the seventeen years.
deep_truth.habit: We call the adult the 'real' animal and the young a stage on the way to the adult. We do this because humans are adults for most of their lives. For a cicada or a mayfly it is the other way round. So the habit comes from our own timetable, and not from nature.
deep_truth.evidence: In Life Bars, the shaded 'young' part was 4 centimetres of the human's 20 centimetre bar, and all but 1 millimetre of the cicada's. The cicada nymph feeds, grows, digs and counts seventeen years. The winged adult lives about four weeks.

three.who_am_i: You are a whole human being now, at the age you are, as a nymph is a whole cicada. Nearly every cell in you carries the full set of instructions for all of you.
three.what_is_life: A life has no single correct shape. It can be seventeen years underground and one month in the air, or one long journey home, or a turning back to the start.
three.what_is_this_world: A salmon builds her body in the sea and leaves it in a mountain forest. The sea, the river, the bear and the tree are joined by her one journey.

roots.thread: Every animal in this unit begins as one cell. That one cell divides and becomes the many kinds of cell in a body: muscle, nerve and skin. All of them carry the same genes, so the one is still present in each of the many. In the immortal jellyfish, the many kinds of cell can go back towards one simple kind and begin again. And a brood of cicadas is millions of separate bodies who count the same years and come up as one crowd.

teachings.teaching: The morning mushroom knows nothing of evening and dawn. The summer cicada knows nothing of spring and autumn.
teachings.link: Zhuangzi chose the cicada as his example of a short life, because he saw only the summer adult. He could not see the years underground. The part of a life that we notice may be only its last small part.
verse: 朝菌不知晦朔，蟪蛄不知春秋。
楚之南有冥靈者，以五百歲爲春，五百歲爲秋。
上古有大椿者，以八千歲爲春，八千歲爲秋。

teachings.teaching: A hen is only an egg's way of making another egg.
teachings.link: Butler turned the usual view round. Seen from the nymph's side, the winged cicada is the nymphs' way of making more nymphs.

teachings.teaching: The one who lives in a body passes through childhood, youth and old age in that body, and then passes on to another body.
teachings.link: The Gita says that something stays the same through all the stages of a life. Science finds one thing that does stay the same from egg to nymph to adult: the genes in every cell. Whether anything more stays the same is a question science has not answered.

science.text: Nearly every cell of a body carries the same full set of genes at every stage of life. John Gurdon showed this with frogs in 1962.
The medusa of Turritopsis dohrnii can turn back into a polyp in the laboratory, again and again.
Whether any animal can avoid growing old altogether is not known.

other_view.view: The adult is the stage that matters most, because only adults breed. Natural selection keeps a way of living only if it ends in surviving young. On this view the nymph's seventeen years exist for the sake of the adult's four weeks, even though they are far longer.

practice.title: A slow look at your own hand
practice.say: Sit comfortably and look at your hand. This hand was once much smaller. Think of one thing it could not do then. Now close your eyes and take five slow breaths. With each breath, notice that you are fully here, at the age you are now. Open your eyes. Tell me one thing you love doing at this age.
practice.kid: Look at your hand. It was once much smaller. Close your eyes. Take five slow breaths. You are fully here, at the age you are. Open your eyes. Say one thing you love doing now.

ask: The nymph is the cicada for seventeen years. So why do we call the winged one the 'real' cicada?
Is your childhood a time of getting ready for life, or is it life already?
A polyp grows from an old medusa, with the same genes. What would have to stay the same for her to be the same animal?
What is the same in you now as when you were a baby?

playtest: The experiments and activities in this unit were reasoned through step by step. They have not yet been tried at home, so please treat the amounts as a starting point. The Crowd Test (core) needs two people, 100 rajma or kabuli chana, a bath towel and a timer. A child usually picks up six to nine in ten seconds. If your bird gets all ten every time, use a bigger towel or seven seconds, and keep that time for the whole test. The Home Stream Test (core) needs a strong-smelling liquid, three matching katoris and four other cups. With vinegar or rose water most noses lose the smell at about 1 in 100 or 1 in 1,000. With vanilla essence it may still be found at 1 in 10,000, and then the step tells you to add one more cup. Rinse the spoon between cups, or the weak cups will be stronger than they should be. The mixtures are for smelling and not for drinking. Life Bars needs only paper and a ruler. The adult part of the cicada's bar is 1 millimetre, and the mayfly's is too thin to measure, which is the point. Run It Backwards and the Egg Budget use atta dough or play clay. Expect 30 to 60 chana-sized eggs. The Salt Switch needs a grown-up to cut the potato, and a 40 minute wait. If the strips show no difference, wait 30 minutes more. Three Survival Curves uses made-up numbers with the true shapes. The Dal Jar Watch works only if you can find pulse beetles in old whole moong, cowpea or chana, so it is an extra and not part of the main path. It takes about five weeks, or up to seven in cool weather. Keep the jar covered and away from stored food. The Fish Pass is wet: use a tray or the bathroom floor. Emerge! needs two to four players and is built on one idea about prime numbers that scientists still argue about, and the game says so. No part of the main path needs a garden. Facts a person may wish to check: the four-year cicada of Meghalaya and the names of the scientists who described her, the figure of about 15 in 100 cicadas eaten by birds, the strength of the smell that salmon followed in the 1970s tests, and how far up the Ganga hilsa once swam. The quotations from Zhuangzi and the Bhagavad Gita are paraphrases. The three films were found by title and channel on YouTube and were not watched from here, so please watch each one first.
